about: Every Claude Code behavior csift depends on, one claim per entry. Each check names the instrument that ran, what it observed and the counting rule; the README badge version is admitted only when every claim carries a check at that version. Never bulk-edit the checks.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded shell launch is an ordinary `type:"assistant"` record carrying a `Bash` (on Windows `PowerShell`) `tool_use` whose input is `{command, description?, timeout?, run_in_background:true, dangerouslyDisableSandbox?}`. Across 2942 corpus launches `description` was present on 99.4% and `timeout` on 25.0%. The flag is NOT exclusive to the two shell tools (the `Agent` tool takes it too, 257 launches) and it is NOT the only way into the background: a FOREGROUND shell command that exceeds its timeout is auto-moved to the background, minting a `backgroundTaskId` with no `run_in_background` on the launching tool_use (80 corpus cases, CC 2.1.210 through 2.1.258).
claims.depends: csift's launch ingester keys on exactly that shape (tool name `Bash` or `PowerShell` plus `input.run_in_background == true`); a renamed input flag would make every background task invisible and collapse the `idle-background-open` verdict.

claims.instrument: `rg -l '"run_in_background":\s*true' ~/.claude/projects --glob '*.jsonl'`, then parse each matching line's `tool_use` blocks. Counting rule: one launch = one `tool_use` block with `name` in {Bash, PowerShell} and `input.run_in_background === true`, keyed by (file, tool_use id) and deduped on that key - a raw line count over-reads because the field is echoed back inside tool_result text.

claims.behavior: The paired `tool_result` for a backgrounded shell opens `Command running in background with ID: <id>. Output is being written to: <abs path>.` and then appends, conditionally, ONE of two notify sentences (`You will be notified when it completes.` on 97.2% of corpus results, or `If it exits while you are still working you will be notified, but it is terminated when you give your final response...` on 1.0%) or neither (1.8%), then usually `To check interim output, use Read on that file path.`, then optionally a `Session cwd remains <path>; directory changes made by the backgrounded command do not apply to subsequent commands.` line (34.0%). The structured `toolUseResult` is `{stdout, stderr, interrupted, isImage, noOutputExpected, backgroundTaskId}` on 51.9% of results, that set plus `backgroundCwdHint` on 33.0%, absent entirely on 13.7% (the subagent lane), and may also carry `assistantAutoBackgrounded`, `backgroundEndsWithFinalResponse` or `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`.
claims.depends: csift lifts the task id after the literal `with ID: ` and the output path after `written to: `, falling back to `toolUseResult.backgroundTaskId` / `taskId`; a reworded result string breaks the text path and leaves the id null on the lanes where the structured field is absent.
claims.instrument: Launch any command with `run_in_background` and read the result record: `csift search 'Command running in background' @<session> --raw | head -1`. Counting rule: one verbatim result string per launch; the unit test `helpers_parse_the_result_text_and_locate_the_main_transcript` in src/live/tests/background_scan.rs pins both markers.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded shell's `tool_result` is a LAUNCH RECEIPT, not a completion. The shell driver first AWAITS the spawn (`xt=await dV(we,d.signal,"bash",{...})`, @165032171); then, when `run_in_background` is true and background is neither disabled nor constraint-forbidden, it awaits task registration and returns `{stdout:"",stderr:"",code:0,interrupted:false,backgroundTaskId}` without awaiting the command's own result promise (@165033229). The result mapper turns that id into the visible tool_result text (@165023434) and the ack formatter writes one of FOUR sentences (@164082185): the explicit `Command running in background with ID: <id>. Output is being written to: <path>.`, a manually-backgrounded variant that also carries `with ID: `, and a moved-to-deliver-a-message and a timed-out variant that both render `(ID: <id>)` instead. So the launch record and its receipt land close together but not instantly, and WHERE the remaining seconds sit is not attributed by any traced hop: the spawn and the registration both happen inside the tool call, so a slow pairing is not the tool idling, and no transcript field records what else intervened (a permission dialog is a named hypothesis, not a finding). Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one delta per (a `Bash`/`PowerShell` tool_use with `input.run_in_background` true, the tool_result block naming that id), both timestamps read off the carrying records: 3216 launches, 3216 paired, min 0.049s, median 0.413s, p90 0.955s, p99 7.389s, max 197.855s - 2915 (90.6%) under 1s, 301 at or over 1s, 51 over 5s and 2 over 30s. Under the looser rule that drops the tool-name restriction the same corpus gives 3487 launches, 3487 paired, median 0.413s, p90 1.003s, max 197.855s. The 2026-09-02 check reported one launch of 2942 that never paired at all; it does not reproduce under either rule today. During the pairing window the launch IS an unreturned call; once paired - the steady state for the whole life of the background command - the tail state machine reports `no pending call`, so a running background shell is invisible to unreturned-call liveness logic.
claims.depends: This is why csift added the whole-file background scan and the seventh verdict `idle-background-open`; before it, a session idling at `end_turn` with a running background build reported `idle-eot` and satisfied `wait --until stop`. Two consequences follow from the receipt shape. Inside the pairing window the same launch is BOTH an unreturned call at the tail and an already-open background row: `background_scan::ingest_launches` builds the row from the launch `tool_use` alone (`id: None`, `state: Open`), so the harness task id is simply missing until the receipt lands. And because only two of the four ack sentences carry the `with ID: ` marker the ingester scrapes, the id for a moved-to-background or a timed-out launch has to come from the structured `toolUseResult.backgroundTaskId` fallback in the same ingester (src/live/background_scan.rs), never from the ack text alone.
claims.instrument: Launch `sleep 600` with `run_in_background`, then run `csift status @<session>`: the tail row reads `no pending call; last stop_reason end_turn` while the verdict is `idle-background-open` with a shell row. Counting rule: one launch, one status read; the e2e test `an_open_background_shell_is_the_seventh_verdict_with_its_row` in tests/cli/live/background.rs pins it against a fixture.

claims.behavior: The async launch ack is not the child's report. The Agent tool's async branch returns a data object that carries no result field - its keys are `isAsync`, `status:"async_launched"`, `agentId`, `description`, `resolvedModel`, `prompt`, `outputFile` and `canReadOutputFile` (@163924487) - and the renderer's `status==="async_launched"` branch, which is gate and writer in one statement, builds an ack text that says in itself that the agent is working in the background and that nothing is known about its results until the notification arrives (@163933514). The child's report arrives LATER as a `<task-notification>` whose `<tool-use-id>` is the SPAWN's own tool_use id: the async branch registers the background task with the tool context's toolUseId (@163923772) and hands that IDENTICAL context object to the agent runner (@163924487), which binds it as its own parameter (@163871668) and whose completion exits pass the same id into the report enqueuer (@163878352); the enqueuer passes it to the shared notification XML builder, which walks a fixed pair list and emits each tag only when its value is truthy (@162044480), so `<tool-use-id>` is present exactly when a launching call id was passed. A pulse with NO `<result>` body is a different object from the ack - the ack is a `tool_result` string, never a pulse - and among the background-task paths this claim covers there are three producers of one: the backgrounded-shell completion notifier, which passes the builder a toolUseId but no body at all (@164968580, in the shell/monitor notifier whose head is @164968006); the Monitor event emitter, whose body is an `<event>` element and which passes neither a status nor a toolUseId (@163710154); and an agent completion whose finalMessage was empty, since the enqueuer emits the `<result>` section only when a final message was passed (`Ie=_?...:""`, @164954168). That is not an exhaustive enumeration of result-less pulses: other callers of the same shared builder emit them too (the remote-agent notifier, the stopped and killed task notices, the resume-time orphan notices). The join is one-to-many, not one-to-one: the agent report's own `<note>` reads, verbatim, `A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.` (@164954168). Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per ack (a tool_result whose text carries `Async agent launched successfully`) joined by `<tool-use-id>` to every `<task-notification>` section in a delivered carrier: 668 acks, 316 joined, 313 of the 316 joined to a result-bearing section, and 316 of 316 with the pulse strictly LATER than its ack (min gap 1.3s, median 486.6s, max 5101.1s). The three joined acks with no `<result>` are the gate itself in the corpus: each is an agent run whose summary reads `failed: Agent terminated early due to an API error`, so no final message existed to emit. Across all carriers only a minority of id-bearing sections carry a result at all (346 of the 1998 user-carrier sections that have a `<tool-use-id>`). The 2026-09-02 check measured the same shape on a smaller corpus: 298 acks, 155 joined, 155 of 155 result-bearing and strictly later, median gap 530.5s.
claims.depends: csift labels the ack `agent.tool.result` only (never a child return) and emits an extra `agent.communication.inbox` view (child to self) for a result-bearing pulse, excerpting the `<result>` body; conflating the two attributes the child's work to the launch instant, and without the id join the report is attributed to nobody and degrades to `?`. A pulse with no `<result>` body - a shell or monitor completion, or an agent completion that produced no final message - correctly gets no communication view at all, and because one task can notify more than once csift must treat the ack-to-pulse join as one-to-many rather than assume a single terminal report.

claims.behavior: A command Monitor is a `local_bash` task in the harness, so its task id is drawn from the SAME `b`-prefixed namespace as a backgrounded shell's; only the tool NAME distinguishes a monitor from a shell.
claims.depends: csift classifies a background row's kind from the tool name, never from the id shape; an id-prefix classifier would mislabel every backgrounded shell as a monitor and merge the two into one id space.

checks.rule: Distinct ids after dedupe on each side; a shared namespace is evidenced by identical length and prefix with disjoint draws, since a per-kind prefix would separate them.
checks.note: Confirmed from both ends. The binary's prefix map has entries for monitor_mcp (`m`) and monitor_ws (`s`) but none for a command monitor, and on disk every one of 427 command-monitor task ids is `b`-led and 9 characters - the same shape and the same namespace as the 2707 backgrounded-shell ids, with zero collisions. So an id-prefix classifier really cannot tell a command monitor from a backgrounded shell, and csift's use of the tool name is the only sound discriminator. claims.behavior: `toolUseResult.backgroundTaskId` is a SECOND join key, never the primary one, and its absence in a subagent lane is not a property of the shell tool. The shell driver's background branch always produces a backgroundTaskId (@165033229) and it rides as one field of the tool's data object (@165030211); whether that object is persisted at all is decided by one predicate - `gPe=(e,n)=>!e.agentId||e.preserveToolUseResults===!0||n.preserveToolUseResultInSubagents===!0` (@162742281) - and the record builder writes `toolUseResult:Ge?je:void 0` (@162940037). So in a subagent lane with no preserve flag the WHOLE object is absent, not merely the key. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one presence/absence observation per (file, launch tool_use id), lane taken from a `subagents` path component, launches restricted to `Bash`/`PowerShell` tool_use blocks with `input.run_in_background` true: 3216 launches, all paired. Main lane 2550 - 2549 carry the key, none carries a `toolUseResult` OBJECT without it, and the single remainder is a user-REJECTED launch whose `toolUseResult` is the STRING `User rejected tool use` on an `is_error` result, so the command never ran and no task id exists. Subagent lane 666 - 350 carry the key and 316 (47.4%) do not, and all 316 have no `toolUseResult` object at all. Earlier runs of the same rule, for comparison: 2026-09-02 gave 350 of 624 with the key and 274 without (43.9%); 2026-09-03 gave 350 with and 284 without; an independent verification on 2026-09-04 gave 350 with and 313 without. The count carrying the key is stable while the count without it grows with the corpus. WHICH spawns leave the preserve flag false is NOT established: two spawn sites pass `preserveToolUseResults:!Oe()` (@163921869 and the resume path @175692688) as the negation of a one-word predicate whose definition sits in another chunk, and the third disjunct is a property of a different tool, so the split inside the subagent lane is observed, not attributed.
claims.depends: csift joins on `<tool-use-id>` first and any `<task-id>` second; making `backgroundTaskId` primary would strand nearly half of subagent-lane launches as permanently open. The gate also fixes what a reader may conclude from the absence: in a subagent lane the missing shape is the whole `toolUseResult` OBJECT, so csift must not treat that object's presence as a precondition for a background launch, and must not read a subagent-lane launch with no structured result as one that failed or never ran. The rejected-launch case is the opposite shape and matters as much: there the `toolUseResult` is a STRING, so a reader that assumes an object must not book that launch as an open background task.

claims.behavior: A background task's completion pulse rides one of THREE carriers, and which one depends on what the session was doing. Every pulse is pushed onto the one session command queue and, unless the item is marked unlogged, logged by the queue's line writer, which builds `{type:"queue-operation", operation, timestamp, sessionId, content?, reason?}` with content and reason present only when supplied (@162031901, entered from the enqueue path @162035411). When the pulse lands while a turn is already in flight, the mid-turn fold consumes the queued items with `reason:"absorbed_mid_turn"` (@164752380) and emits each as a `{type:"queued_command", prompt:<the notification XML>, commandMode:"task-notification", ...}` attachment (@165734734); no `type:"user"` record is written on that path. When the session was idle the pulse is delivered as a `type:"user"` string record instead. The queue's operation vocabulary is FIVE names, enumerated at the ten call sites of the line writer inside the queue factory and re-grepped 2026-09-04: `enqueue` (@162035321, @162035826, @162037718), `dequeue` (@162037953, @162038474, @162038598, @162039004, every one called bare with neither content nor reason), `remove` (@162039411, inside the filter-remove @162039241, and the ONLY site that passes a reason argument at all), `popAll` (@162041308) and `popOne` (@162041776). A reason-less `remove` is therefore that same filter-remove entered with an undefined reason through its discard and consume wrappers, and never a dequeue, which logs its own operation name. `clearCommandQueue` (@162039491) is not one of those paths: it forwards its own options to the discard wrapper (`dr(()=>!0,Br)`) and its sole call site passes `{reason:"cleared_on_cancel"}` (@180832280), a reason that appears nowhere in this corpus. Census 2026-09-04, one observation per `type:"queue-operation"` line over every transcript under the projects root: 13,868 lines - enqueue 6938 (all with content, none with a reason), dequeue 3542 (never content, never a reason), remove 3279 (2262 with content and no reason, 796 with neither, 209 `absorbed_mid_turn`, 12 `delivered_to_agent`), popAll 109, popOne 0. Of 2549 main-lane background-shell launches that returned a task id, 1036 (40.6%) have no `type:"user"` carrier naming that id anywhere - 1022 have a queue or attachment carrier instead and 14 have no carrier at all; the 2026-09-02 check measured 1015 of 2520 (40.3%) under the same rule.
claims.depends: csift's carrier ingester reads all three carrier shapes; restricting it to `type:"user"` records loses 40% of shell completions, leaving them permanently `open` and flipping the `idle-background-open` verdict. The reason field is an explanation, not a state: a reason-less `remove` is the ordinary case, so csift must not read the absence of `absorbed_mid_turn` as evidence that a user record was written, and its `[remove . reason]` label zone renders a reason only when the writer supplied one. `dequeue` and `popAll` are separate operations rather than reason-less removes, so a census that buckets queue lines by operation must carry all five names.
claims.instrument: Take a known background task id from a launch result and `rg -n '<that id>' <the main transcript>`, then classify each matching line by its top-level `type`. Counting rule: one carrier observation per matching line, bucketed into `queue-operation` / `attachment` / `user`; a launch with no `user` row but a `queue-operation` row is a mid-turn delivery.

claims.behavior: A background task launched from a subagent lane is CLOSED by a carrier in the PARENT main transcript, and the cause is the SINK, not the addressing. The pulse itself is addressed to the launching lane: the backgrounded shell's exit callback fires the completion notifier with the agent id the task was registered under (@164973293), and that notifier addresses its enqueue inline as the owning agent id falling back to the root (@164968716). It never goes through the shared addressing helper, whose call sites are exactly three - the agent-completion enqueuer (@164953647), the workflow notifier (@168826340) and the agent-resume path (@175694140) - beside its definition (@164954861); a whole-binary enumeration of that helper returns those four occurrences and no shell-path use. Nor is a child-addressed pulse absorbed by the main thread: the per-lane fold admits, on the main thread, only items whose agentId equals the root id, and in a child lane only `task-notification` items addressed to that child (@162030912, with the main-thread predicate `agentId === root` at @160411638). So a child-launched shell's pulse can be addressed to that child and never delivered in the main lane at all. What lands in the root file regardless is the QUEUE line: the queue factory builds every queue-operation record with the CURRENT (root) session id and no agentId key (@162031901), the write-policy table gives `queue-operation` the `always` policy while only content-replacement, fork-context-ref and observer-ref are route-by-agent (@166067281), and the store's append defaults its session id to the store's own session and sends an `always` record to that session file (@166106795, routing switch @166107428) - so the enqueue and remove lines are written to the root session file whatever agent the notification was addressed to, and no queue carrier can be diverted into a subagent transcript. Measured 2026-09-03 over the subagent transcripts under the projects root (7,761 at that run): 638 subagent-lane background-shell launches, 633 distinct task ids, 622 closed by at least one carrier in the parent, and ALL 622 carry a queue-operation enqueue line with zero closed without one; an independent run the same day gave 641 launches and 625 closed. Notifications are not strictly absent from subagent transcripts: when the wake router delivers one to an IDLE agent (@179256565) the resume driver mints it in that agent's own transcript as an `isMeta:true` user record (@175692385), and a SECOND child-lane shape exists, a `queued_command` attachment - over those same launches 6 task ids carried the user record and 5 the attachment, so both child-lane counts are floors, not totals (an earlier count on 2026-09-02 recorded 12 isMeta user records in 5 child files, builds 2.1.159 through 2.1.258, under a per-record rather than per-task rule). Every such delivery is also on the parent's queue-operation enqueue and remove line, so a main-only carrier read still sees all of them.
claims.depends: csift reads launches from every lane but carriers only from the main transcript, resolving the main file from a subagent target; scoping the notification index per file instead of per session root inflated never-returned from 24 to 631, a 26x false-positive rate. The main-only carrier read is sound precisely because the closing evidence is the queue line rather than a delivered pulse: a pulse addressed to a child that never wakes still leaves its enqueue and remove lines in the root file, and the fold guarantees the main thread will not absorb it. A child-lane delivery (the isMeta user record, or the queued_command attachment) is therefore an ADDITIONAL shape csift may see, never a closure it would otherwise miss.
claims.instrument: Take a background id launched inside a `subagents/agent-*.jsonl` and `rg -c '<that id>'` in the child file against the parent transcript: the completion appears only in the parent. Counting rule: one launch per (file, tool_use id), `rg -c` counting matching lines; the e2e test `subagent_launches_complete_in_the_parent_main_transcript` in src/live/tests/background_scan.rs pins it.

claims.behavior: A Monitor produces TWO notification shapes, from two different call sites. An EVENT pulse carries only (task-id, summary, event): the monitor's stdout sink is a token bucket (ten tokens, one refilled every 2000 ms) whose data handler calls the event emitter once per admitted line (@163709751), and that emitter builds its notification with a task id, a `Monitor event: "<description>"` summary and an `<event>` body, passing NO status and NO tool-use id (@163710154), so under the shared builder's truthiness rule a pulse cannot carry `<status>` (@162044480). The SAME status-less emitter also writes the housekeeping notices: the arm's timeout callback sends the notice beginning `[Monitor timed out` (@168332544), and the sink sends its own suppression notice and, after 30s of sustained overflow, a stopped-for-too-much-output notice while killing the task (@163709751). A timeout is therefore NOT distinguishable from an ordinary event by tag shape - only by the literal text of the event payload. A TERMINATION notice is the other shape: on shell exit the completion notifier writes (task-id, tool-use-id, output-file, status, summary) with the monitor-specific summary heads `Monitor "..." stream ended`, `... ended without producing output`, `... script failed` and `... stopped` (@164967491). Corpus 2026-09-04, one observation per `<task-notification>` section in a delivered `type:"user"` record whose `<summary>` begins with the word Monitor, over every transcript under the projects root: 1017 sections - 114 termination notices with `<status>` completed in 114 of 114 (no failed or killed termination appears), and 903 status-less pulses, every one carrying an `<event>`, of which 13 are the timeout notice and 890 are ordinary events; no suppression and no stopped-for-output notice appears in this corpus, and no section carries neither a status nor an event. The 2026-09-02 check measured 111 of 111 completed and 841 pulses under the same rule.
claims.depends: csift keeps a monitor OPEN through event pulses (a carrier with no `<status>` and no timeout event leaves the state untouched) and closes it only on the termination notice or a timeout event; treating a pulse as a completion closes a persistent monitor on its first event. Because the timeout notice is shape-identical to an ordinary pulse, csift's close-on-timeout test is necessarily a substring test on the `<event>` payload, which is the only signal available; the sink's two other housekeeping notices ride the same status-less shape and are correctly left non-closing, since the stopped-for-output case also kills the shell and so produces its own status-bearing termination notice. The rendered label likewise falls back to the `<event>` payload instead of fabricating `completed`.

claims.behavior: Almost every armed monitor notifies; the widely quoted 30% is a carrier-restriction artefact, not a failure rate. The armed set is published in exactly one place, the arm's result text `Monitor started (task <9-character id>, persistent - runs until TaskStop or session end | timeout <n>ms). ...` (@168334560). Every pulse then goes through the one session queue, which logs an enqueue line carrying the notification text (@163710154 into @162031901), while only the un-folded items become `type:"user"` records: the mid-turn fold consumes the rest as attachments with `reason:"absorbed_mid_turn"` (@164752380). Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, with armed ids read only from that arm template inside a tool_result and fired ids taken from every `<task-id>` inside any `<task-notification>` section on all three carriers: 448 distinct armed task ids, of which 12 (2.7%) never appear in any notification at all - including a stop notice, which would itself be a notification section carrying the task id - and of those 12, seven were armed persistent and five with a timeout; two of the twelve carry fixture-shaped repeating ids quoted inside tool output, so 12 is a ceiling. Restricting the fired set to notifications delivered as a `type:"user"` record raises the silent count to 136 of 448 (30.4%). The 2026-09-02 check gave 7 of 430 (1.6%) and 129 of 430 (30.0%) under the same two rules, so the user-record-only figure is the stable one at about 30% while the all-carrier figure is small in both runs. The residue is NOT attributed: a persistent monitor that never emits a line and never exits has no writer to fire, and a timeout-armed monitor whose session ended before its timeout has none either, but neither explanation has been confirmed per id.
claims.depends: csift reports an armed monitor as `open` with the explicit honesty note rather than inferring it is still live; absence of an event is never evidence of absence, and a persistent monitor must never be reported as failed. The carrier restriction is the trap the claim exists to name: any census of monitor liveness that counts only delivered `type:"user"` records will report roughly a third of armed monitors as silent, so csift's background scan must read the queue-operation and attachment carriers too, and the module doc's parenthetical `30% of armed monitors produced no notification at all` needs to read `no user-record notification`.

Counting rule: one reconciliation record per matching line; a record with N real ids plus one `__orphan_summary__:` sentinel reconciles N tasks.

claims.behavior: Agent orphans branch three ways - handed to auto-resume, `stopped`, or `failed`. Auto-resume requires FOUR conditions together, not two: an auto-resume callback is present, the agent was launched by the Agent tool or by a forked skill, its meta is fetchable, and its transcript mtime is younger than 172800000 ms (48 hours). A notification enqueued with mode:"task-notification" reaches the drain, which computes kn=N6(po.origin)??(po.mode==="task-notification"?{kind:"task-notification"}:void 0) and Fo=po.isMeta||!Vw(kn)?"system":po.inputSource??De (drain @181584368; Vw(e){return e===void 0||e.kind==="human"} @160108907, so a task-notification origin is never human and the field is stamped "system" on this path), and passes both to the builder xe, which returns {type:"user", message:{role:"user", content: e||up}, ..., origin, promptSource} with the content it was handed - the notification template STRING, which is why message.content is never an array here (@165935440). The persisted line then spreads ...Gjt(sessionId) over the record, whose userType is the constant "external" (@166105359, Gjt/Ymn @166074085). Two fields the old text treated as part of this shape are NOT stamped by this path at all: isSidechain is insertMessageChain's own caller-supplied parameter (isSidechain:n) and isMeta rides in from the queued command (the drain passes isMeta:po.isMeta), so neither is a property of the notice. claims.behavior: Two interrupt bindings share one handler: chat:cancel (escape) always calls pn({gesture:"escape",suppressBackgroundAgentKill:true}), while the global app:interrupt (ctrl_c) handler passes that flag only in the viewing-an-agent branch and otherwise calls pn({gesture:"ctrl_c"}) bare (@180831002). Inside pn the kill routine is reached only under if(!wn&&(_o||ci||h3e())) where wn is suppressBackgroundAgentKill (@180829485), so escape provably cannot kill. The routine filters the task registry by she(T)=fr(T)&&(T.status==="running"||Dm(T))||T.type==="in_process_teammate"&&T.status==="running" - fr is type==="local_agent", Dm is completed-with-pending-work - and no shell, monitor, workflow or remote kind appears in it (@180827798); the constant j4e=3000 declared on the same line is both the double-press chord window and the confirm toast timeout. The routine kills each admitted entry and enqueues the gesture's only on-disk trace, `Background agent "<d>" was stopped by the user.` or `<n> background agents were stopped by the user: ...`, with mode:"task-notification" (@180828701). What the predicate does not settle, and what this claim therefore does not assert: the same branch first calls a wake-registry reset - mz(tt,{durable:false}) (@168768925) opens with p3(),ALe(), where p3 (@163691727) walks every entry of the wake registry clearing its coalesce timer, rescanWanted, pendingConfirm, pendingSeed, idle-rescan cancel and read-retry timer and bumps cancelGeneration, and ALe (@163692217) bumps scanGeneration - so whether an ARMED Monitor still fires after the gesture is not decided by the kill predicate alone. The survival of a backgrounded shell process after an interrupt has never been observed here either; it needs the live trial the instrument names. Corpus 2026-09-04: 10 stopped-by-the-user notices in the whole corpus (9 plural, 1 singular), all classified harness.notification.subagent, none naming a shell or a monitor.
claims.depends: csift's idle-background-open verdict treats an open shell or monitor as still open after an interrupt; assuming the interrupt closed everything produces a false idle-eot, and the resume path starts with an empty in-memory task list so survivors surface only as orphans. The kill predicate backs that reading for shells and monitors to the extent that the kill routine never touches them; it does not license reading an open monitor row as a promise that the monitor will fire again, since the same branch resets the wake registry. csift's row is a report of a launch with no completion carrier, which is exactly what it should stay.

claims.behavior: A never-returned background launch is usually far from EOF but not always, and the numbers move with the corpus, so they carry their scope and date. Sweep of 2026-09-04 over 65 top-level sessions and 3912 launches (completed 3595, failed 114, killed 83, open 93, timed_out 19, stopped 8): 93 launches never returned (60 monitors, 25 shells, 8 agents) and all 93 were located. Distance to EOF, all kinds: min 0.0 MB / 4 lines, median 48.1 MB / 22940 lines, max 502.8 MB / 146275 lines; 78 of 93 (84%) sit beyond a 512 KB tail window and 15 sit inside it. Shells alone (n=25): min 0.0 MB, median 10.5 MB / 3780 lines, max 375.5 MB / 109866 lines, 14 of 25 beyond. Agents (n=8): median 4.1 MB, max 268.1 MB, 7 of 8 beyond. Monitors (n=60): median 49.1 MB / 25200 lines, max 502.8 MB, 57 of 60 beyond. The earlier sweep of 2026-09-02 measured the same shape at a smaller scope (63 sessions, 3849 launches, 88 never-returned, 74 of 88 beyond the window) and added two figures not re-measured since: 84 of those 88 were launched more than a day before their session's last record, and among launches that DID return, 4.7% (84 of 1805 main-lane launches with a locatable completion) were more than 512 KB from their completion. No harness code computes or writes such a distance; the 512 KB window is the consumer's own constant, so this claim is a corpus measurement with a counting rule and no producer to find.
claims.depends: csift's background report is a whole-file scan behind a byte prefilter (measured +0.2-0.4 s worst case) rather than a tail read, because a 512 KB tail window misses 84 percent of the never-returned population (78 of 93 today) - not all of it, since 15 sit inside the window - and a tail-only implementation therefore reports zero open tasks on any long session.

claims.behavior: The harness writes NOTHING about a still-running background SHELL at end of turn: the 2.1.258 turn_duration record factory emits only durationMs, budgetTokens, budgetLimit, budgetNudges, messageCount, pendingBackgroundAgentCount and pendingWorkflowCount, and neither pending count can ever include a shell - the counter buckets a live task into pendingAgents only when it is a non-main-session local_agent with isBackgrounded set, and into pendingWorkflows only when its type is local_workflow, while a background shell is type local_bash and a Monitor is monitor_mcp/monitor_ws. Across 4637 turn_duration records on this corpus the 9 observed key sets contain no shell field of any kind. Such records ARE written while background work is open: on a replay of 4638 observations, 4375 had at least one background shell open, 1920 at least one async agent, 2232 at least one async workflow.
claims.depends: csift never reads an end-of-turn telemetry record as proof the session is done and scans the whole main transcript for launches and completions instead; this hole is exactly what the `idle-background-open` verdict fills.

claims.behavior: pendingBackgroundAgentCount on a turn_duration record is never emitted as the literal 0 - the emitter writes `k>0?k:void 0` so a zero count becomes undefined and is dropped from the JSON, and absence of the key therefore means zero. The field does NOT track a transcript-derived set of launched-but-unreturned agents: it is a snapshot of the harness's live in-memory task map (a task counts when its status is running, or when it is terminal but not yet notified), so a transcript replay disagrees with it in both directions - on this corpus the field matched the replayed open-agent set in only 25 of the 136 records that carry it, reading LOWER than the replay 102 times and HIGHER 9 times.
claims.depends: any consumer reading the field must treat an absent key as 0 rather than as unknown; the residual under-count comes from agents that notified and were resumed (a notification is not terminal) and from agents spawned in a child lane.
claims.instrument: `rg -c '"pendingBackgroundAgentCount":\s*0' ~/.claude/projects --glob '*.jsonl'` returns no matches while `rg -c '"pendingBackgroundAgentCount"'` returns many. Counting rule: one matching line = one record.

claims.behavior: ScheduleWakeup puts NO id on the wire. At 2.1.258 the tool takes {delaySeconds, prompt, reason, noop} - noop is a fourth REQUIRED field, thrown for by name ("`noop` is required when `stop` is not true.") and described as "noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak" - or the {stop:true} form; delaySeconds is clamped to [60, 3600] and wasClamped reports the clamp. Its declared output schema K0o (164196846) has exactly five members, {scheduledFor, clampedDelaySeconds, wasClamped, stopped?, cancelledWakeups?}, and no id; all three exits of the tool's call() (164198473) return only those members - the stop:true early return {scheduledFor:0, clampedDelaySeconds:0, wasClamped:!1, stopped:!0, cancelledWakeups:yYn()}, the aged-out return {scheduledFor:0, clampedDelaySeconds:0, wasClamped:!1}, and the normal return copied off the scheduler. The wakeup the tool arms DOES carry an id internally: the scheduler entry is minted as Z5({id:x(),cron:M,prompt:o,createdAt:C,kind:"loop",scheduledFor:k,reason:i,...}) at 160535315, and stop:true cancels those entries by id (DL(o.map((l)=>l.id)) inside yYn at 160534240, whose returned count becomes cancelledWakeups). That id never leaves the process: it appears in no tool input, no toolUseResult and no fire record, so a scheduled wakeup can never be joined to a later notification by id. Re-measured 2026-09-04 over the projects root: 562 ScheduleWakeup tool_use blocks (561 with input keys {delaySeconds, prompt, reason}, 1 with {stop}), 562 paired toolUseResult observations (561 with {clampedDelaySeconds, scheduledFor, wasClamped}, 1 with those plus {stopped, cancelledWakeups}), and 459 scheduled_task_fire records carrying a single key set (content, cwd, entrypoint, gitBranch, isMeta, isSidechain, parentUuid, sessionId, slug, subtype, timestamp, type, userType, uuid, version). No id-shaped key occurs in any of the three.
claims.depends: csift's background scanner does not model ScheduleWakeup; its cadence pulses reach the taxonomy only as harness.schedule.wakeup / harness.notification.monitor records, never as background tasks. Because the arming id never crosses the wire, csift cannot and must not join a scheduled wakeup to the pulse that later fires - there is no join key to build one from, in either direction.

claims.behavior: The task tools persist ONE JSON file per task under a per-list directory at <claude-home>/tasks/<sanitized list id>/<task id>.json (Xk and F @160149333), and TWO directory-name forms exist on real disks because the list id falls through: lA() returns env CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID, else the team name, else the inherited or leader team name, else the session id (@160149333), while session-team init names a team session-<first 8 of the session id> and, when that differs from the session id, RENAMES tasks/<session-uuid> to tasks/<team name> with the rejection swallowed (@183052390) - a best-effort rename, so a uuid-form directory can survive either because team init never ran or because the rename failed, and which cause produced any given survivor is not decidable from the code. The TaskCreate handler writes {subject, description, activeForm, status:"pending", owner: undefined, blocks: [], blockedBy: [], metadata} (@164395722); createTask writes {id: String(highWaterMark+1), ...fields} and updateTask writes {...existing, ...patch, id} through JSON.stringify(...,null,2) (@160151613, @160153498), which is why ids are STRINGS and blocks/blockedBy are always present as lists while activeForm, owner and metadata are optional. The status set is CLOSED, not open: the shipped schema is {id, subject, description, activeForm?, owner?, status, blocks, blockedBy, metadata?} with status the three-value enum ["pending","in_progress","completed"] (@160147000, @160147053), and both readers validate with it and return null after logging "[Tasks] Task <id> failed schema validation" (@160152647, @160153204), so a file carrying a fourth value is dropped by the harness itself. Whether any writer outside this module can land such a value is unread. Corpus 2026-09-04: 184 directories (168 session-form, 16 uuid-form, nothing else), 423 task files; id a string 423/423; blocks and blockedBy lists 423/423; status completed 279, pending 114, in_progress 30 - only the three schema values; activeForm present 337 and absent 86, owner 36, metadata 34; five key sets (271, 82, 34, 32, 4).
claims.depends: csift reads BOTH directory forms and merges them, renders anything that is not `completed` as an open row with its verbatim status (in_progress first, with blockers) and folds completed ones to a count; probing only one form silently reports no tasks for a session using the other, and a numeric-id assumption would drop rows. Rendering the status verbatim rather than through an enum of its own costs nothing today - the harness's reader enforces the same three values - and is what would keep csift honest if a fourth value ever appeared, but it is a csift tolerance choice, not a property of the store.
claims.instrument: `ls ~/.claude/tasks | sed 's/^session-.*/session-form/' | sort | uniq -c` shows both forms; `jq -r .status ~/.claude/tasks/*/*.json | sort | uniq -c` gives the status census; `csift status @<session> --format json | jq '{tasks, tasks_completed}'` prints the rows (null = no dir, [] = a dir with nothing). Counting rule: one row per non-completed task file across both directory forms.

claims.depends: csift's bash operand resolution needs NO cross-command state: each record carries its own spawn cwd, so `files`/`recover` join a relative operand against the carrying record's own `cwd` at the zero-inference `cwd-joined` class, in a subagent lane exactly as in the main thread. A shared-shell model would attribute operands to the wrong directory, and an absent `cwd` would degrade every such row to `unresolved`.

claims.behavior: Claude Code recovers a Bash call's ending directory by appending `pwd -P >| <tmp>/claude-<id>-cwd` as the last element of an `&&`-joined command chain and reading that file back; because the read-back is `&&`-chained, a command that exits non-zero never advances the tracked cwd (the file is never written, the read throws, the tracker is left alone). The read-back result is consumed only under `if(result && !pinned && !result.backgroundTaskId)`, so a backgrounded command is excluded by an explicit `backgroundTaskId` gate and a PINNED lane (any subagent lane) is excluded outright. Under a sandbox the file is named `cwd-<id>` in the sandbox temp dir instead.
claims.depends: csift can trust the record `cwd` as the shell's true spawn directory without replaying exit status; the lexical `cd` inference is applied only INSIDE one command and is labelled `cd-tracked`, so a `cd` that failed at runtime never silently relocates later operand resolution.
claims.instrument: `strings` over the installed Claude Code binary for 2.1.258, grepping for `pwd -P` and the `claude-`...`-cwd` tempfile template: expect one read-back site, `&&`-chained. Live check: run `cd /tmp && false` in one Bash call, then `csift show @main --turn -1 --raw | jq -r .cwd` on the next record - the value must be unchanged. Counting rule: one tracked value per completed call.

claims.behavior: toolUseResult.returnCodeInterpretation is not a generic non-zero marker. On the BASH tool it is computed once per result (165026240) by a dispatcher Gzo (164982483) that takes the first token of the last top-level segment, routes git grep and git diff to the grep and diff interpreters, and otherwise looks the token up in a CLOSED eight-entry table Wzo (164982047): grep, rg, egrep and fgrep to "No matches found", find to "Some directories were inaccessible", diff to "Files differ", and test and [ to "Condition is false". Every entry is built by one factory, x$=(e)=>(n,r,o)=>({isError:n>=2,message:n===1?e:void 0}), so a message exists at exit code exactly 1 and that exit is classified NON-error; every other command falls to the default jzo=(e,n,r)=>({isError:e!==0,message:e!==0?`Command failed with exit code ${e}`:void 0}), which marks the call an error and produces a message the field never carries, since the field is written as returnCodeInterpretation:z?.message (165030298) and undefined is dropped. Absence therefore says nothing about the exit status. The word "only" is scoped to the Bash tool: the Windows PowerShell tool carries a SECOND table of its own in a separate module (176493320) with a different non-error rule (isError:n!==0&&n!==1) and its own values - grep, rg, egrep, fgrep and findstr to "No matches found", a robocopy interpreter that yields a message at exit 0 as well as at 1 to 7, and where, fc and diff for native .exe commands - written at 176593762; those two are the only writers of the field in the binary. Re-measured 2026-09-04 over the projects root, which is macOS-recorded throughout: 259 records carry the key (94 of them in subagent lanes) with exactly three distinct values, all from the Bash table - "No matches found" 252, "Files differ" 6, "Some directories were inaccessible" 1 - and none of the 259 is flagged is_error, as the factory's disjoint isError rule predicts. The transcript keeps only the assistant's unreturned `tool_use` block, and no per-lane control file records the prompt; the ONE disk projection is SESSION-coarse - the top-level session's registry row at `<sessions dir>/<pid>.json`, into which the status patch merges `{status, waitingFor}` while a dialog is open, adding a `statusUpdatedAt` whenever `status` is present (`l$e` at 158821838 forwarding to the pid-file merge `Sn`, which resolves `${process.pid}.json` under the sessions dir and merges the patch into the existing row, at 158820494). `waitingFor` IS persisted while the dialog is up: it is a free-text label from a per-dialog-kind map whose default is the literal `permission prompt` (`fvt(T){return T===void 0?void 0:zS[T]?.waitingFor??"permission prompt"}` at 181515856), and the row reader accepts it verbatim as a string (159697821). It names neither the tool, the tool_use id, nor the lane. So on disk an escalation-blocked lane, a slow tool and a wedged one still share ONE per-lane signature: an assistant `tool_use` block with no `tool_result` for its `tool_use_id`. That block carries exactly FIVE keys, {type, id, name, input, caller}: 223,406 of 223,406 blocks WRITTEN BY THE SHIPPED BINARY carried that key set on 2026-09-03, a block read fresh on 2026-09-04 shows the same five with `caller {"type":"direct"}`, and the only four-key blocks in the whole corpus (137) are records csift's own elicitation sidecar wrote. No permission, escalation, isEscalated or requires_approval field appears on any block; the four-key form {type, id, name, input} is the API WIRE shape, produced by the request normalizer that strips `caller` before sending (`gYn` at 165948669, whose only call site is the request builder). The signature is the UNRETURNED BLOCK, not a stop_reason value: `stop_reason:"tool_use"` is a top-level-lane truth (59,772 of 59,787 records) but holds for only about half of subagent-lane records (85,437 of 163,636; the rest carry a null stop_reason, some with an apiBlockIndex) - both counts 2026-09-03.

claims.behavior: The harness's own definition of an absolute path enumerates exactly three families - a leading /, a <letter>: drive prefix, and a \\-led UNC path - and that enumeration is the harness's, not an inference from data. The msys-to-native translator pair fE/the (157586967) branches on startsWith("\\\\") and on /^([A-Za-z]):[/\\]/ and on nothing else, and the single absolutizer ct (157587730), through which every harness-side path resolution runs, converts an msys /c/... spelling back to native on Windows and then decides absoluteness with node's win32 isAbsolute. The path Claude Code itself WRITES in native form is the record cwd: Gjt (166074084) stamps cwd:ne(), a value normalized on the way into the tracked slot, so on Windows the stamp is the C:\... form. The structured tool fields are not harness-written. input.file_path and toolUseResult.filePath carry the MODEL's own string: the only normalizer over a tool input, backfillObservableInput feeding ct, is discarded unless it ADDS a key (164727722 replaces the block's input only when Object.keys(s_).some((nu)=>!(nu in Mh))), and the Write tool's result literal writes the raw input as filePath:e (163988510) while only the telemetry call receives the ct()-absolutized copy. claims.behavior: A measured minority of shell calls mutates a persistent file, and an in-place `sed` never yields a deterministic literal-subset content anchor. Rate: 9,996 of 119,110 shell tool_use records (8.39 percent) carried at least one real-path bash mutation row under csift's own classifier on 2026-09-02, counting one record per distinct (transcript, line) carrying a mutation row with a non-null resolution; re-measured on 2026-09-04 the rate is rule-sensitive but stable in kind - 8.51 percent (11,528 of 135,483 blocks) under a strict lexical rule, 12.10 percent (15,886 of 131,238 records) under csift's own classifier when class-marker rows (git:, interp:, pkg:, extract:, fmt:) are counted as mutations too, and 19.99 percent under a generous rule adding package-manager, build and redirection shapes. sed: 292 commands carrying 397 `sed -i` invocations on 2026-09-02, and 251 commands with 318 invocations on 2026-09-04 under a rule counting one invocation per sed occurrence carrying `-i` or `--in-place` (a looser rule that also accepts combined flags and heredoc bodies returns more, so the figure travels with its rule); the fully literal s/OLD/NEW/ pairs, neither side carrying a regex metacharacter, were 55 and 36 respectively. ZERO of them is a content anchor, and the harness makes that structural rather than incidental. At approval time the permission preview rewrites the tool input to carry an internal `_simulatedSedEdit:{filePath,newContent,baseHash}` unless the target is a network path, is not writable, is unreadable because too large, or the edit is too large to preview (176215480); the shell tool's very first statement short-circuits on exactly that field and applies the edit in process (`if(e._simulatedSedEdit&&!n.remoteCall)return Hqo(e._simulatedSedEdit,n,o)` at 165023880); and the applied path returns `{data:{stdout:"",stderr:"",interrupted:!1}}` after a file-history touch, with a sed-shaped stderr on a missing file (165018430). The model-facing schema omits the internal field in BOTH of its branches (the published schema is the internal one with `_simulatedSedEdit` omitted, and `run_in_background` omitted as well where the background form is unavailable, at 165013450), so no model-authored command can carry it and the corpus can never specimen the intercept. Even when the harness itself knows the resulting bytes, the tool_result it writes carries none of them - and a shell-run `sed -i` exits 0 whether or not it matched.
claims.depends: csift's bash content anchors deliberately exclude `sed -i`, `tail`, variable targets and interpreter/ssh heredocs; the anchor classifier admits `sed` only in the windowed-read idiom, so an in-place sed can never reach the anchor path at all. The bash resolution work raised full-target attribution from 27.1 percent to a measured 77.0 percent ceiling; those two attribution figures are the bash-resolution work's own and were not re-measured in this audit.
claims.instrument: Collect every `sed -i` Bash command in the corpus (`csift search 'sed -i' <scope> -t agent.tool.use`) and inspect each for an extractable literal old/new pair. Counting rule: commands carrying a literal replacement subset over all `sed -i` commands; mutating calls over all Bash calls.

The shell driver computes cn=Ll()||constraints.background==="forbidden" and Ot=!cn&&OSr(we) (byte 165032058) and registers the promotion only under if(xt.onTimeout&&Ot) (byte 165033132). Output is being written to: <path>.` (byte 164082185). The schema description of the optional member reads `Set when the command hit its timeout and was auto-backgrounded; the timeout value in ms`. When Ot is FALSE - background tasks disabled, forbidden by the caller, or a command OSr refuses (a non-simple parse, or a first word in the denylist ["sleep"]) - nothing is armed and the same timer KILLS the command: exit code 143 (the constant vvt at byte 161445121), the note `Command timed out after <duration>` written only on the timeout kill (byte 161449100), and the call is persisted as a STRING toolUseResult whose head is `Error: Exit code 143` + newline + that note, with is_error true on the tool_result block, no backgroundTaskId and no timedOutAfterMs. Measured 2026-09-04 over the whole projects root (8408 transcripts): 61 promoted echoes, 61 of 61 with a backgroundTaskId, 61 of 61 with empty stdout AND empty stderr, 0 interrupted, 61 of 61 carrying the moved-to-background sentence, 0 of 61 launched with run_in_background; applied limits 120000 x41, 600000 x10, 300000 x6, 420000 x3, 180000 x1, across 14 builds, none of them yet 2.1.258. claims.behavior: The foreground Bash timeout is the call's own `input.timeout` clamped to a ceiling of 600,000 ms, defaulting to 120,000 ms when the call names none (the binary carries the pair as adjacent constants `120000` and `600000`). Both bounds are overridable per environment by `BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` and `BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`, both on the settings `env` allowlist, and on a main-agent lane that can auto-background `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_BACKGROUND_TIMEOUT_MS` lowers the effective limit further to `min(requested, max(env, 2000))`.
claims.depends: csift never predicts how long a lane may legitimately sit at an unreturned Bash `tool_use`: `agents` reports `pending_classification: awaiting-execution` and hands the caller `pending_since_utc` to weigh. The ceiling is what makes that weighing possible on a lane where auto-backgrounding applies - past ten minutes the harness's own timeout path would have returned a background promotion, so continued silence points at a blocked or abandoned lane rather than a slow command.

claims.behavior: This claim carries two facts, and only the second is about Claude Code. (1) A READING-TOOL invariant with no Claude Code producer and none possible: csift's label taxonomy is exactly 34 leaf classes (33 at 0.10.0; `harness.meta.system` added in 0.10.1) across three roles - 5 under user, 5 under agent plus 3 under agent.communication, and 21 under harness - and `agent.thinking` is the ONLY leaf whose dotted path is a segment-prefix of another leaf (`agent.thinking.narration`). Re-counted at csift 0.10.3 today from the value-parser error's full dotted paths, bare roles and mid-path prefixes excluded: 34. The count is a property of csift's own enum, so no binary site can ever produce it. (2) What those leaves must COVER, which IS a Claude Code fact: a whole-corpus census on 2026-09-04 over 7,944 transcripts - top-level and subagent alike, workflow journal files and csift's own elicitation sidecars excluded and reported apart - found 1,370,953 non-blank lines, 0 unparseable, 0 without a top-level `type`, and 18 distinct top-level types, of which 133,258 lines (9.72 percent) belong to types no leaf models: the deliberately unpromoted session-state cache lines (last-prompt, permission-mode, mode, ai-title, agent-name) plus six unmodeled types totalling 2,642 lines - atis-latch 1,216, bridge-session 1,148, history-suppression 226, fork-context-ref 33, cost-state 18, continued-in 1. Four of those six carry no uuid and no timestamp and belong with the bookkeeping lines; two carry an instant (history-suppression via `ts`, continued-in via `timestamp`) and are the only leaf candidates. The mapped/unmapped split applies a TYPE-level rule to LINE counts - a type counts mapped when at least one leaf models a record of it - so the 13,830 queue-operation lines ride in the mapped total although only the content-bearing ones classify. The corpus is live: the same census on 2026-09-03 returned the same 18 types over 1,346,372 lines with 132,965 unmapped (9.9 percent), so the totals are dated snapshots while the type SET is stable. Earlier figures of nineteen types over 2,627,138 lines with 265,322 unmapped (10.1 percent) were a double count - each line booked once per session and again in a summary - and are withdrawn. On the Claude Code side only one leaf family currently has a connected trigger, gate and writer: harness.notification, from the local background-shell completion handler that mints a background-command pulse (164968441) through the shared pulse builder whose per-tag truthiness loop decides which tags reach disk (162044480) to the user-record constructor whose return literal becomes the line bytes (165936023).

Neither reports whether the model received the content. The only branch in which `isMeta` decides a record's fate is inside the transcript-to-messages assembler, which SKIPS a record only when isMeta is set AND its origin is absent or `unclassified` (`if(xt.isMeta&&tEn(Ot))continue` at 165543739 with `tEn(e){return e===void 0||e.kind==="unclassified"}` at 160108958); isMeta alone never removes a record, and that assembler's readable consumer is the auto-mode classifier's view builder. No traced API-request-path filter reads either flag, and for `isVisibleInTranscriptOnly` the negative is closed by enumeration: the property read `.isVisibleInTranscriptOnly` has exactly 7 sites in the 2.1.258 binary, all above byte 155,000,000, each read today - 162047661 a last-human-turn walk-back, 163579541 the SDK stream synthesis bit, 165931677 and 165935120 two prompt/record predicates, 165941036 a record-copy builder that re-spreads the flags into the user-record factory, 166033146 the display filter, 180531636 the UI prompt-text cache - and none assembles a request payload; for `isMeta` the survey is a grep of the property read `.isMeta` (129 sites in the binary today, 128 of them above that offset; the bare token `isMeta` returns 382) in which none sits on a request path. claims.behavior: Claude Code concatenates several harness sections into ONE `type:"user"` record, and the two batching paths are SEPARATE - they never produce sibling sections of different families. Peer batching: the inbox poller hands every pending message to the peer formatter at once, which wraps each in its own section and joins them with a blank line, prepending the relay preamble ONCE for the whole batch - so one record can hold several inbound peer sections of mixed kind (prose, `idle_notification`, `teammate_terminated`). Notification batching: the wake router groups every queued task-notification for one idle agent and joins their values with a blank line into a single prompt, which the resume driver mints as ONE isMeta user record with the automated-event framing applied once. A whole-corpus census on 2026-09-03 over 7,837 transcripts found 3,794 string-content user records carrying at least one section close and 127 multi-section records: 123 pure peer batches (the largest holding 29 sections) and exactly TWO pure notification batches, of 2 and 3 pulses, both in subagent lanes, each carrying the framing once, 494 characters before the first tag, with pulses separated by exactly one blank line. No record carries a notification section as a SIBLING of a peer section. The two records that hold tags of both families are QUOTING, a third and separate case: a `<task-notification>` tag sits inside a `<teammate-message>` BODY, which the peer writer leaves unescaped because its masking replaces only the section's OWN tag name. The mirror case - a peer tag quoted inside a notification body, which the notification builder appends unmasked - is a PRODUCER fact with ZERO specimens: exactly one `<task-notification>` span in the corpus contains a peer tag, and that span carries no `<result>` element at all.
claims.depends: csift recognizes a section only at a BOUNDARY (content start, immediately after the relay preamble, or right after a prior section's close tag), which is what makes the quoted case safe: a tag inside a section BODY is not at a boundary, so it starts no section and the carrying record keeps its own family. csift scans ALL sections and UNIONs their labels, with notification precedence over a peer tag quoted inside a notification span - a defensive rule that is producer-sourced and still unobserved - mirrors that masking exactly in the per-section text render so classification and render never drift, and emits one hit per section. A plain `contains` check mislabels any genuine message that merely quotes a tag mid-prose, common in csift's own development sessions.

claims.behavior: When background agents are killed from the UI, Claude Code writes a plain-STRING type:"user" notice in one of two templates, built in a single statement (byte 180829177) from a list pushed from each killed task's description: the singular `Background agent "<desc>" was stopped by the user.` or the plural `N background agents were stopped by the user: "<desc>", "<desc>".`. Because the templates interpolate only a count and those descriptions, no agent id can appear - measured 2026-09-04, 0 of 10 corpus notices carry a >=16-hex token. The scope of that negative is the Background agent family only: a sibling notice for a killed task (byte 166018828) writes `Task "<description>" (<taskId>) was stopped by the user.` with isMeta true and DOES name an id. The notice is handed to the pending-notification queue as {agentId, value, mode:"task-notification", skipAttachments:!0} (byte 180829290) with NO shouldQuery flag - unlike the resume orphan writer at byte 178956727, which passes shouldQuery:!1 - so the delivery path does not mark the notice passive and does not by itself suppress a generation. That no assistant record follows any of the notices is a corpus observation about the NEXT record, not a property the path enforces: measured 2026-09-04 on the 10 specimens (1 singular, 9 plural), the following record is a file-history-snapshot on 3, a user record on 3 and an attachment on 4, and an assistant record on 0.
claims.depends: csift treats the notice as a synthetic marker so it is excluded from `is_genuine_user` and never opens a turn, classifies it `harness.notification.subagent`, and renders `[subagent stopped] <notice>`; without the exclusion each kill inflates the human-turn count (9 corpus specimens were previously read as `user.message`). Because the Background agent notice names no id, `csift status` can report that agents were stopped but not WHICH - a limit that does not extend to the killed-task notice, which carries its taskId in the text. The raw needle `stopped by the user` doubles as the verifiable synth marker guarding the whole-file prefilter gate, and it is deliberately broader than the notices: re-run 2026-09-04 the phrase matches 1243 records across 10 labels, of which exactly 10 land under `harness.notification.subagent` and none under `user.message`. csift must not read the notice as evidence that the turn ended: the delivery path passes no suppression flag, so any future surface inferring 'no generation followed' has to look at the following record, not at the notice.
claims.instrument: csift search 'stopped by the user' --count-by label, asserting the user.message key is absent and that the harness.notification.subagent count equals the on-disk notice count. Do NOT assert that every matched record lands under harness.notification.subagent: the phrase also occurs in ordinary prose, and corpus-wide the query returns 242 records across 9 labels of which only 10 are notices (agent.tool.result 122, agent.tool.use 60, agent.thinking 29, agent.communication.inbox 10, harness.notification.subagent 10, agent.message 8, agent.communication.sent 4, harness.compaction.summary 2, harness.meta.attachment 1).

claims.behavior: An asynchronous background Agent spawn's tool_result is a LAUNCH ACK, not the child's report: its text opens 'Async agent launched successfully' and it carries structured toolUseResult.{isAsync:true, status:"async_launched"} under the spawn's own tool_use_id (272 records corpus-wide, both signals on all of them); the child's actual report arrives LATER as a <task-notification> pulse carrying a <result>. The structured status:"async_launched" marker is broader than this family - a further 174 records are background WORKFLOW launches carrying that status with no isAsync key and the different ack text 'Workflow launched in background. Task ID: <id>'.
claims.depends: csift prefers the structured signal and falls back to the text prefix (`Record::is_async_launch_ack`), labeling the ack `agent.tool.result` ONLY and excluding it from subagent-return detection, while the later `<result>`-bearing pulse is what additionally carries `agent.communication.inbox` with direction child to self; conflating them attributes the child's report to the launch instant.
claims.instrument: `jq -r 'select(.toolUseResult.status=="async_launched") | .toolUseResult.agentId' <file> | wc -l` versus `grep -c 'Async agent launched successfully' <file>`, then `csift search 'Async agent launched' --format json | jq -r '.label'` must be `agent.tool.result` on every row and never `agent.communication.inbox`. Counting rule: one ack per launch, one inbox record per `<result>` pulse.

claims.behavior: Claude Code's promoted non-record lines carry no text spelling out their rendered facts: a `turn_duration` record is {durationMs, messageCount} integers plus ids, `stop_hook_summary` is {hookCount, hookInfos, hookErrors, preventedContinuation} and `file-history-*` are paths and version numbers - 0 of 284 turn_duration, 0 of 410 stop_hook_summary and 0 of 139 file-history-delta records contain the bracketed strings csift renders. csift fabricates FOUR such forms, not three: `[turn duration: ...]`, `[stop hooks: ...]`, `[file-history delta at ...]` and `[file-history snapshot at ...]`, the last two both under the single `harness.meta.snapshot` marker `file-history-`.
claims.depends: csift registers each line's own type/subtype bytes (`turn_duration`, `stop_hook_summary`, `file-history-`) as VERIFIABLE synthesized-text markers, active only under the explicit selector that admits the line; without a marker the whole-file prefilter gate would silently drop matches against those fabricated excerpts. The queued and away-summary leaves render VERBATIM content and need no marker.
claims.instrument: `csift search 'turn duration' . -t harness.meta.turn-duration -c` must return hits (measured 270 exchanges over 284 records) while a per-RECORD probe shows 0 of 284 turn_duration records contain the phrase in their raw bytes. Counting rule: exchanges for csift, records for the probe. Do NOT use a whole-file `rg -c 'turn duration'` as the negative side - it returns 56 on a transcript whose prose discusses the feature.

checks.observed: Per-record probe over one project dir's top-level .jsonl: turn_duration 284 records, 0 whose raw line contains 'turn duration' (with the space); stop_hook_summary 410 records, 0 containing 'stop hooks'; file-history-delta 139 records, 0 containing 'file-history delta at'. A raw turn_duration record is fields only: {type, subtype, durationMs: 446815, messageCount: 105, timestamp, uuid, isMeta, userType, entrypoint, cwd, sessionId, version, gitBranch}. csift renders the fabricated excerpts: '[turn duration: 10m 29s . durationMs=629054 messageCount=266]', '[stop hooks: count=6 errors=0 prevented=false]', '[file-history delta at 2026-07-14T03:00:27.193Z: <path>@v1]', '[file-history snapshot at <ts>: <path>@v2, ...]'. `csift search 'turn duration' . -t harness.meta.turn-duration -c` = 270 (exchanges; several turn_duration records share a turn, so 270 exchanges cover 284 records). The by-file rg, however, returns 56 - the phrase occurs as ordinary prose in a corpus that documents the feature. away_summary renders VERBATIM record content (observed: the summary sentence itself, no bracket), consistent with it needing no marker.
checks.rule: Restrict to the promoted records themselves, not the file: of the N records whose parsed (type, subtype) is the promoted kind, count those whose RAW line contains the rendered phrase - expect 0/N (measured 0/284, 0/410, 0/139). claims.behavior: Optional fields ride the compaction boundary record, and whether isMeta rides it depends on WHICH constructor the lane used, not on what the record means. Both constructors coexist in 2.1.258: the local one (Sce at 166031907) writes isMeta:!1 literally, the stream-event one (Ugt at 163581237) has no isMeta key at all, and the byte writer is JSON.stringify plus a newline, which drops undefined keys - so the key is simply absent rather than false. A corpus census on 2026-09-04 over 235 boundaries: 101 carry an isMeta key and its value is false on 101 of 101, true on 0 of 235; 3 carry agentId and those 3 are exactly the isSidechain:true subagent boundaries (all at version 2.1.219); 1 carries sessionKind with value bg (at 2.1.252), which the envelope builder stamps from the CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KIND env read (158816699) that returns a value only for a background or daemon job. By version, the isMeta-bearing rows are 98 main-thread boundaries stamped 2.1.150 through 2.1.191 plus the 3 subagent rows at 2.1.219, while all 134 isMeta-less rows are stamped 2.1.199 through 2.1.259, 2.1.258 and 2.1.259 included; at 2.1.219 the two lanes disagree in the same build (2 main-lane rows without the key, 3 subagent rows with it). The flip is a ROUTING change, not a constructor change: both constructors coexist from 2.1.191 on, but there the isMeta-less arm is unreachable from an ordinary REPL because no engine ships (tengu_shoji_engine and CLAUDE_CODE_SHOJI_ENGINE have 0 occurrences in 2.1.191, re-measured 2026-09-04), while 2.1.193 is the first shipped build carrying that engine and its gate (env CLAUDE_CODE_SHOJI_ENGINE or the statsig flag, default false, at 212468279) whose boundary arm (215011271) rebuilds the record without isMeta. So 2.1.193 is a CAPABILITY floor with the gate defaulting false into 2.1.199, the observed flip is bracketed by the corpus at 2.1.191 (present) and 2.1.199 (absent), and by 2.1.258 the engine literals are gone from the binary while the isMeta-less stream arm is the live path.

In 2.1.258 the literal occurs 14 times: one constant-table entry, seven write or propagate sites (the two compaction-summary constructions at 164805869 and 164834461, the partial-compaction branch at 164840615, the user-record builder's parameter and object literal at 165935532 and 165936147, and the per-block re-wrap at 165941009 and 165941037) and six readers. claims.behavior: A compaction summary is a turn MEMBER, not a turn delimiter, so a backward walk from EOF passes through compaction boundaries transparently. How DEEP the window reaches is budget-relative, and the depth is a measured-at-a-moment figure rather than a constant: at the default 40,000-char budget on the five most compaction-heavy top-level transcripts the crossings were 1/80, 4/33, 5/32, 2/15 and 10/11 on 2026-09-02 and 1/80, 4/33, 3/32, 2/15 and 10/11 on 2026-09-04, the third session having moved because a live session keeps growing above its newest boundary and the budget is then spent higher up. The pattern the tuple illustrates is what is stable: a session whose turns are long spends the budget before the first boundary (1 of 80), a session of short turns crosses nearly all of them (10 of 11, i.e. up to 10 boundaries inside one 40K reconstruction). The two ways of counting agree in every run: the emitted `compaction_boundary` row count equalled the header's `boundaries_spanned` in all five sessions on 2026-09-04 and in all five on 2026-09-02.
claims.depends: `verbatim`'s recency-first selection reaches back across multiple compactions by default (`--max-compactions N` caps the crossing count, demonstrated by the 10/11 session falling to 1 spanned under `--max-compactions 2`) and banners every crossed summary; treating a summary as a delimiter would stop the reconstruction at the newest boundary. Because the crossing depth is budget-relative and moves as a live session grows, no csift surface may treat a particular depth as fixed - the header's `boundaries_spanned` beside `boundaries_total` is the reported pair, and the boundary row's line key is `line`, not `line_no`.
claims.instrument: csift verbatim @<session> --budget 40000 --format json | jq -rc 'select(.kind=="compaction_boundary")|.line' | wc -l, cross-checked against the header row's boundaries_spanned and boundaries_total. Counting rule: boundaries the budget window crossed over the session's total. NOTE the boundary row's line key is `line`, not `line_no` (the row carries exactly kind/line/summary_chars), so the ledger's `.line_no` projection yields null on every row.

claims.behavior: A transcript whose FIRST TIMESTAMPED record is a system/compact_boundary was minted by COPYING another session at that compaction point. The ingress is the background-job fork: the launcher builds the child argv with a NEW --session-id plus --fork-session and --resume of the origin (167454405) and stamps CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KIND=bg into the child env (167454816), the resume walk rebuilds the array backwards from the leaf and stops where a record has no parent - which the writer forces on a boundary - so the forked array HEADS with the newest boundary, and the new session id has an empty already-written uuid set, so every loaded record is re-appended as if new. The copy therefore preserves the origin's record uuids, timestamps, parentUuid and logicalParentUuid, rewrites sessionId, ADDS sessionKind, STRIPS the slug (the per-session slug cache has no entry under the new id, so the key is undefined and the serializer drops it) and stamps the COPYING build's own version - which is why copied records carry timestamps predating the file itself. The other conceivable ingress, a rebuild from replayed frames, is excluded twice over by its own converter (163578140): its system arm keeps only compact_boundary and its default arm returns nothing, so no attachment, turn_duration or stop_hook_summary record can come out of it, AND it restamps every record it rebuilds with a fresh timestamp (system arm at 163579247), so it can never yield a head boundary that is uuid- AND timestamp-identical to the origin. Corpus census 2026-09-04 over 68 top-level transcripts: the first timestamped record is attachment on 64, queue-operation on 2, system/compact_boundary on exactly 1 (at line 28, behind 27 untimestamped bookkeeping lines) and absent entirely on 1 file that carries no timestamped record; csift flags exactly the boundary-headed file, with a resolved origin, and flags neither queue-operation head - zero false positives.

claims.behavior: File birthtime is NOT a fork signal. Measured over 64 top-level transcripts, the birthtime is LATER than the first record on 64 of 64 (filesystem copies and migrations move birthtimes past the records; the largest ordinary gap is 45d17h, the median 4h13m). The true fork's gap is only 15h19m and ranks 27th of 64, so any 'first record much older than birthtime' threshold that catches the fork also fires on 26 ordinary transcripts. Comparing a UTC record timestamp against a LOCAL birthtime additionally inflates the delta by the zone offset - the same 15h19m gap reads as 25h19m.
claims.depends: csift's clone law calls no `stat()`, reads no birthtime and trusts no clock, so it never reports an ordinary migrated transcript as a fork; the structural head-record rule is the whole instrument.
claims.instrument: For each top-level transcript compute first_record_ts_utc - birthtime_utc with BOTH operands in UTC, sort descending, and locate the known fork's rank. Counting rule: one delta per file; the refutation number is the count of non-forked files whose delta exceeds the fork's (26 of 63 here), which is threshold-free.
