claims.behavior: A clone's head `compact_boundary` is a RE-SERIALIZED copy of the origin's, not a byte copy - and the verbatim survival is a statement about THAT LINE, not about every copied record. On the head boundary (re-measured 2026-09-04): 14 fields are byte-identical - uuid, logicalParentUuid, parentUuid, timestamp, compactMetadata, content, cwd, entrypoint, gitBranch, isSidechain, level, subtype, type, userType - and 4 are rewritten at copy time: sessionId to the clone's own, slug present to absent, sessionKind absent to "bg", version stamped with the COPYING build (2.1.252 against the origin's 2.1.251). The mechanism is a record-by-record rewrite by a child process rather than a file copy: the fork is spawned with --session-id <new> --fork-session --resume <origin> (byte 167454405) under CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KIND "bg" (byte 167454922); the append writer spreads the loaded record over a freshly computed envelope and then re-stamps sessionKind, userType, entrypoint, cwd, sessionId and version on every append (bytes 166105359 and 166074085), while the slug is looked up in the per-session cache under the NEW id, comes back undefined and is dropped by serialization (byte 166104737). Across the copy as a whole the identity fields do NOT all survive. Of the 558 uuids the clone shares with its origin: timestamp survives 558 of 558, no copy carries a slug, parentUuid survives only 556 of 558, and 2 of the 161 usage-comparable shared assistant records arrive with the four top-level counters (input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens) zeroed while message.usage.iterations and message.usage.cache_creation keep the origin's real figures (2, 2973, 2140, 962321) - the origin holding exactly ONE line for each of those uuids, which rules out reading a zeroed line off disk. All three exceptions are the LOAD-time relink inside the forked child (byte 166141698, invoked once as the loader accumulator's finish at byte 166188605): it re-chains the boundary's preserved uuids from anchorUuid so the FIRST preserved record's parentUuid becomes the anchor, re-parents whatever ELSE pointed at the anchor to the LAST preserved uuid, and zeroes those four counters on preserved ASSISTANT records only. The disk matches rule for rule: this boundary's compactMetadata.preservedMessages carries a 7-entry `uuids` list - the list the relink walks - beside a 9-entry `allUuids`; the two zeroed records are `uuids` entries 0 and 1, the only two preserved uuids present in the copy as assistants; and of the two parentUuid rewrites one is `uuids` entry 0 re-parented to anchorUuid while the other is an attachment record that appears in NEITHER list, re-parented to the last preserved uuid. Because the boundary uuid itself survives the copy it identifies the origin - but only under the join criterion, not as a raw byte match: sweeping the clone's project tree for that uuid on 2026-09-04 (759 .jsonl files) returns THREE files by raw grep - the clone, the origin, and one subagent transcript whose 3 hits are prose mentions (0 as a record's own uuid, 0 as a parentUuid, 0 as a logicalParentUuid) - while exactly TWO files, the clone and the origin, carry it as a record's OWN uuid on a record that is itself a compact_boundary.
claims.depends: csift's origin join (session::clone_origin) demands the uuid appear as a record's OWN uuid on a record that is itself a `compact_boundary`, so a prose mention of the uuid or a `logicalParentUuid` back-reference is refused and a co-clone (whose head probe returns the same boundary uuid) is skipped; the sweep is one memmem pass over the DIRECT parent directory's sibling .jsonl files - a read_dir, never recursive, so the subagent transcript that now carries the uuid in prose is not even opened - and it is paid only when a clone was detected. That join, not the raw byte match, is what keeps the answer at one origin on today's corpus, and the third file is the live demonstration of why the join is written the way it is. The relink is also why 'shares a uuid' must never be read as 'is the same record' anywhere else in csift: a clone double-counts its inherited records on every spanning surface until scoped away, and the two zeroed copies are absorbed by `stats`' per-field MAX dedupe over message.id rather than by any identity assumption. The discriminating instrument for a future audit: the compaction-time zeroer (byte 163630561) spreads message.usage and overrides the same four counters but cannot touch parentUuid, so a record that is BOTH re-parented and zeroed is the load-time relink, with the origin's line count for that uuid as the secondary check.

claims.behavior: A transcript can carry the SAME uuid on more than one line - a replay of records already written - and a replayed copy can arrive with its top-level usage zeroed (input_tokens, output_tokens and both cache counters at 0) while the real numbers survive inside usage.iterations, so usage is not always identical within one message.id. Corpus census 2026-09-04: 13 of 68 top-level transcripts hold duplicate uuids, 9,131 in total, and every duplicated line is stamped between 2.1.159 and 2.1.220 (2.1.159, 2.1.191, 2.1.199, 2.1.202, 2.1.206, 2.1.208, 2.1.210, 2.1.211, 2.1.220) with none newer - so this is a shape a reader must still tolerate in older transcripts rather than a description of current behaviour. The same census fixes the shape's frequency: the second copy always keeps the timestamp (0 pairs differ anywhere in the corpus), frequently carries a different parentUuid (610 of 1,327 and 554 of 1,175 in the two largest duplicate-bearing files), and only rarely carries zeroed usage - 6 records corpus-wide, in 2 files, of which 3 are also re-parented. The zeroed variant is the LOAD-side relink's signature (hns at 166141698: the head of the boundary's preserved list re-parented to the anchorUuid and the preserved ASSISTANT records zeroed on exactly the four counters the zeroing helper ude at 163630561 overrides while spreading the rest of message.usage), not only the compaction-time re-anchor - and in 2.1.258 the compaction-time re-anchor (163631022) has no call site in the main REPL lane at all. Specimen re-read today: three assistant records sharing one message.id at lines 27860-27862 reappear at 29136-29138 with byte-identical timestamps, the head of the replayed triple re-parented, all three top-level usage tuples (0, 0, 0, 0) and usage.iterations[0] still carrying {input_tokens 2, output_tokens 708, cache_read_input_tokens 474834, cache_creation_input_tokens 3997}.
claims.depends: csift's token dedupe takes a per-field MAX across an id's records rather than first-wins (src/stats.rs): identical on clean data, immune to the zeroed replay, and commutative so the rayon fold stays correct; first-wins would make the reported total depend on traversal order, and it breaks in the opposite direction on the other measured shape, a mid-stream partial where output_tokens rises from 2 to 1404 inside one id. The duplicate-uuid replay also means any per-file uuid index must tolerate more than one record per uuid, and a diff between two copies of a record must not treat a parentUuid difference as corruption.
claims.instrument: Group a transcript's records by `message.id` and flag ids whose members disagree on any usage field; count duplicate uuids per file alongside. Counting rule: per id, per file. Measured over the 6 largest top-level transcripts: 4 had 0 mismatching ids, 1 had exactly 1 (a duplicate-uuid replay whose second copy is all-zero at the top level while usage.iterations keeps the real numbers), and 1 had exactly 1 of a different shape (a mid-stream partial, output_tokens 2 -> 1404, in a file with no duplicate uuids). Duplicate uuids themselves are common (474, 464, 250, 1175 in four of the six files), so the replay is frequent and the ZEROED replay is the rare variant.

claims.behavior: A compaction does NOT rewrite the transcript: Claude Code APPENDS a `type:"system"` `subtype:"compact_boundary"` record and then, on the VERY NEXT line, a `type:"user"` `isCompactSummary:true` `isVisibleInTranscriptOnly:true` record, so every pre-compaction line number stays valid and the pre-compaction records stay in the same file below the boundary. The boundary is the append point and the summary is always boundary+1 (13 of 13 events measured); the transcript writer is an append call (`appendEntryToFileAsync`), never a rewrite of earlier lines.
claims.depends: The whole `Lnnnn` addressing contract rests on it: `verbatim` reconstructs the clipped turns out of the SAME file (its crossed-summary banner names the summary's own line and says the turns below predate it), a `csift show --line` refetch printed before a compaction still resolves the identical record afterwards, and `image`'s stable id `L<line>i<n>` is stable for exactly this reason. If compaction rewrote or renumbered the file, every stored line address in a prior answer would go stale.
claims.instrument: Note a pre-compaction record's `Lnnnn` from any csift surface, let the session compact, then re-run `csift show @<id> --line <that same line> --format json`: it must return the identical record (same `uuid`). Then `csift search '' @<id> -t harness.compaction.boundary --format json | jq -r '.hits[].line'` must be greater than every pre-compaction line, and the summary's line must be exactly one greater than the boundary's. NOTE the jq path: search JSON nests matches inside `{"hits":[...]}` exchange rows, so a top-level `.line` selects nothing. Counting rule: one boundary record plus one immediately following summary record appended per compaction event; line numbers are 1-based and per file.

claims.behavior: Claude Code synthesizes the AskUserQuestion tool_result from a ladder over the recorded answers, an optional freeform response and an idle timeout, and that ladder gained a fifth outcome at 2.1.216. In 2.1.215 and below it is FOUR-way: an idle timeout first (the 'No response after Ns ...' text, optionally followed by 'Before going idle the user had selected: <rendered>.'), else a non-blank freeform response ('The user responded: <text>'), else any rendered answer string, UNCONDITIONALLY prefixed 'Your questions have been answered: <rendered>. You can now continue with these answers in mind.', else 'The user did not answer the questions.' From 2.1.216 the answered arm SPLITS on a predicate over every question - no notes recorded AND the recorded answer is one of the offered labels (for a multiSelect question, a non-empty set of offered labels; an unanswered question passes) - keeping the old prefix when the predicate holds and writing 'The user answered: <rendered>. Read the answers carefully - they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed - and follow what they actually say.' otherwise. Measured 2026-09-04: the literal 'The user answered: ' has 0 occurrences in 2.1.215 and 2 in both 2.1.216 and 2.1.258, while the other four templates are present in all three; 2.1.215 and 2.1.216 are adjacent entries in the published version list, so the boundary is as tight as that list allows. The retired phrasing 'User has answered your questions' is absent from 2.1.191 through 2.1.259, so its removal predates this range and cannot be dated here. On disk, a user.answer census on 2026-09-04 returns 100 carriers: 81 lead with 'Your questions have been answered' (record versions 2.1.156 through 2.1.258), 18 with 'The user answered:' (2.1.217 through 2.1.259), and 1 apparent match of the retired phrase that is not an answer at all but a subagent tool_result whose content BEGINS with that phrase as the first row of a marker-count table.
claims.depends: csift recognises an AUQ answer by START-anchored prefix (trim_start plus starts_with) against a LIST of markers, four since v0.10.3: the retired 'User has answered your questions' (kept for historical transcripts), 'Your questions have been answered', 'The user answered:' and the freeform 'The user responded:'. The list is the FALLBACK for records without toolUseResult - the primary boundary signals are a non-empty toolUseResult.answers or, since v0.10.3, a non-blank toolUseResult.response - and 'The user did not answer the questions.' is deliberately excluded because it opens no turn, as is the idle-timeout text. A single hardcoded marker missed the dominant form entirely and silently dropped real user.answer turns, while a contains check false-positived on any tool result that merely QUOTES a marker. The version reading is the practical consequence: a single-prefix list is complete for transcripts written by 2.1.215 and below and lossy from 2.1.216 onward. One measured caveat on the START anchor: it still admits a record whose content OPENS with a marker as quoted text (exactly one such record in the corpus today), so the structured toolUseResult signals must stay primary. All four phrasings are also verifiable synth markers in the search prefilter. The marker list's doc comment in src/model/markers.rs is stale on both counts - it says CC has shipped THREE phrasings and dates 'The user answered:' to 2.1.258, against a four-entry list and a measured 2.1.216 floor.

claims.behavior: A PENDING AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode is never flushed to the transcript while it waits: Claude Code buffers the WHOLE assistant turn and commits the `tool_use` to the persisted message array only after the interactive tool resolves (verified across 51 sessions with zero counterexamples; on one measured session the ask's `tool_use` was still absent from disk 37 minutes after its own emit timestamp, and the answering `tool_result` landed about 89 minutes after that timestamp). If such a `tool_use` is on disk, its answer is too - so an option-picker freeze is byte-identical on disk to a stall.
claims.depends: csift cannot render a pending-question state from the native transcript at all; the unanswered window is recoverable only from the hook-written sidecar, whose unresolved pendings `search`/`show`/`verbatim`/`list` merge as if native (a pending marker classifies `agent.tool.use`, renders `(elicitation sidecar)` in place of a line number, and every surface that merged one prints `with elicitation sidecar`). A `status` that inferred 'blocked on a question' from the transcript alone would be fabricating.
claims.instrument: With an AskUserQuestion open on screen, run `csift search AskUserQuestion @<that session> -t agent.tool.use` from another terminal: zero native hits while pending. Re-run after answering and the tool_use appears, timestamped at its EMIT instant rather than the answer instant. Counting rule: one record per tool_use block. Requires a live session - it cannot be observed from a static corpus.

claims.behavior: Whether an AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode tool_use is on disk while its dialog is open is a TIMING outcome of the persistence frontier - not a question-count rule, and not a change made at 2.1.258. In 2.1.258 the stream loop creates one assistant record per content block, the message_delta event then fills stop_reason on every record of the turn before any tool runs, and the write frontier (166067641: while a response is in flight, stop at the first assistant record whose stop_reason is still null, otherwise the whole array is eligible) therefore releases the ask record the moment the API turn ends; the recorder is an effect whose content dependency is the message-array identity (181643343), so an eligible record reaches disk at the next change of that array, and an in-place field mutation alone schedules nothing. Nothing on that path branches on how many questions an ask carries: the persistence path branches only on stop_reason, on the in-flight flag, on the store array identity and on isLoading, and as supporting evidence the byte substrings 'questions.length' and 'questions?.length' occur 0 times in 2.1.257, 2.1.258 and 2.1.259 while '.questions' occurs exactly 36 times in each, with all 36 in 2.1.258 read and none in the persistence path (that needle set cannot see a count test on a destructured binding - the dialog's own submit path reads such a binding near 181429402 - which is why the negative rests on the read of the write path and the enumeration only supports it). The 2.1.258 boundary is refuted as well: the frontier body is byte-identical in 2.1.257 and 2.1.258 and only minifier-renamed in 2.1.259, and the isResponseInFlight literal enters at 2.1.233 as a recorder-class options-bag rename over an unchanged body, so it dates a refactor. What has actually been measured is a shape, not a rule: in two live trials at 2.1.258 (macOS and a Windows 11 ARM64 guest) an unreturned tool_use whose input.questions held two elements was on disk while the picker sat on question 1, and a single-question ask raised in the same sessions stayed unwritten. The retrospective corpus cannot decide the differential: of 114 AskUserQuestion tool_use blocks readable today, 92 carry one question and 17 carry two to four (spanning record versions 2.1.156 to 2.1.258), ZERO are unreturned (every one of the 137 hits csift labels agent.tool.use for that tool is paired), and the ask/answer order probe leaves 90 of 98 pairs undecidable with every discriminating record a queue-operation line - so no version origin is asserted.
claims.depends: status and wait carry the tail dialog as its own HITL leg beside the registry waiting row and the elicitation sidecar, and the evidence line says which leg fired. The derivation is sound and unchanged: tail_dialog (src/live/verdict.rs 299-302) fires on ANY unreturned AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode at the tail and never counts questions, so a pending ask that reached disk is seen without the sidecar while one that did not is still attributed to the sidecar or to the registry row. What is wrong is the JUSTIFICATION csift carries: the comment at src/live/verdict.rs 291-295 and the note emitted under that leg (the string at 347-350) both tell the reader that a multi-question ask is written at question time since CC 2.1.258 while a single-question ask stays buffered - a rule the binary does not implement. The honest wording is that a pending dialog is on disk only when the API turn had already ended and something changed the message array during the wait, so the absence of a tail dialog is never evidence that no dialog is open, and the presence of one is not evidence about how many questions it asks. The claim's code sites need moving too: 170-227 and 255-262 are the pid- and sidecar-evidence blocks and do not hold this claim; the load-bearing site is the tail-dialog block at 291-302.

claims.behavior: An assistant record reaches disk on a schedule set by the streaming turn, not by the tool it announces, which is why a tool_use can sit on disk with no tool_result. In 2.1.258 the API stream loop builds one assistant record per completed content block - a fresh uuid, the emit timestamp, stop_reason still null - pushes it into the turn's record array and YIELDS it at block completion, before any tool runs (@165443045, @165443533). When the API turn ends, the message_delta arm assigns usage, stop_reason and stop_details IN PLACE on every record already in that array (@165444727); that is what releases the persist frontier, whose body is `if(!r)return e.length;` followed by a walk that stops at the first assistant record with a null stop_reason (@166067641, exported as transcriptCursorEnd at @174418867). Eligibility is not the write. The yielded record reaches the REPL through the streamed-message router and the append arm of _applyMessage (@181620972, @181617981, @181619681), and the write itself is an effect record(messages,{ignore,isResponseInFlight,teamName,selfAgentName,storageV5}) over a seven-entry dependency list (@181643343). THREE of those dependencies vary within a turn at the call site NHe($ie,$ie.length===mh?.length,HC) (@181878008): the messages array identity, the ignore flag (that live length comparison) and isResponseInFlight, bound as HC=Ue(Ui,vDo) with vDo(x){return x.isLoading} (@181865175, @181858491). So an already-eligible record is written when that effect next re-runs, whichever of the three moves - and when isResponseInFlight is false the frontier returns the whole array. The recorder then slices from the already-recorded floor to the frontier and hands the slice to the chain writer (@181641798), which builds the on-disk envelope (parentUuid, logicalParentUuid, isSidechain, agentId, gitBranch, slug spread over the record) and appends the line (@166105359). Nothing on that path branches on how many questions an AskUserQuestion carries: questions.length has ZERO byte occurrences in every cached build probed today (2.1.23, 2.1.100, 2.1.124, 2.1.152, 2.1.198, 2.1.228, 2.1.233, 2.1.252, 2.1.258, 2.1.259), the frontier body matches byte-for-byte in shape from 2.1.100 through 2.1.259 and is absent at 2.1.23, and the isResponseInFlight literal first appears at 2.1.233 as an options-bag rename over that same body - a refactor date, not a behaviour date. Specimen, 2026-09-04: 68 top-level transcripts, of which exactly 1 ends permanently at an unreturned assistant tool_use carrying stop_reason "tool_use" (counting rule: one transcript per top-level session file, i.e. a .jsonl directly under a project directory; a frozen tail is a last user/assistant record that is an assistant record with a tool_use block whose id appears in no tool_result in the same file). That witness and the earlier live self-probe are both lanes that keep replacing the conversation array; a lane blocked on an APPROVAL dialog has not been observed, and the traced dependency list leaves two further ways such a lane's record could still be written (an isLoading flip, or a change in the ignore comparison), so the blocked-dialog case is neither confirmed nor excluded here.
claims.depends: lifecycle's frozen-lane detection and status's in-flight verdict both read an unreturned tool_use at the tail as a live block rather than a clean finish (status forced Running, never completed); if the assistant commit were deferred until the tool returned, a blocked lane would look like an end-of-turn idle. The ordering above makes that sound for any lane that keeps producing records. It is NOT a receipt for the approval-dialog lane, so csift's frozen-lane classification must keep its current caution: escalation-blocked is the one state jsonl can positively confirm and awaiting-execution stays an honest can't-tell. One csift correction rides this claim: the comment at src/live/verdict.rs 291-295 (and AGENTS.md section 3.4) asserts that a MULTI-question AskUserQuestion is written at question time since Claude Code 2.1.258 while a single-question ask stays buffered - that sentence has no producer and must be withdrawn. The code it annotates does not branch on question count (tail_dialog tests only the tool name against AskUserQuestion / ExitPlanMode), so no behaviour changes; only the justification does.

claims.behavior: Claude Code recomputes a hook payload's session_id and transcript_path on every dispatch rather than caching them at bootstrap. The shared base builder Sa(session, cwd, permissionMode, options) returns {session_id:e.id, transcript_path:lm(e.id), cwd:n, scratchpad_dir, prompt_id, permission_mode:r, agent_id:o?.agentId, agent_type, effort} (2.1.258 @165808976), and lm builds a FLAT <projects>/<encoded>/<sessionId>.jsonl, never a subagents/ path (@166068377) - so on every locally dispatched hook both fields name the TOP-LEVEL session. The one exception is inside Sa itself: an early return for a served remote call yields session_id:`served:${callerSessionId ?? "unknown"}` with an EMPTY transcript_path (@165808976). That branch is out of reach for the two MCP elicitation hooks, because their payload builders call Sa with THREE arguments - _Ee for Elicitation (@165797748) and its twin yEe for ElicitationResult - so the options bag is undefined and both remoteCall and agent_id are undefined; PreToolUse by contrast passes a fourth argument (@162932581). The session object those builders hand in is minted fresh as {id:Q(), project:{originalCwd, projectRoot}} (@184439575) from the top-level session getter, even when the elicitation/create request arrived from inside a subagent (@184438640). 2.1.258 also adds a sibling field that DOES name a subagent's own transcript: agent_transcript_path:Ud(d), constructed only in the SubagentStop arm of the Stop payload builder (@165803380); of the field's 12 byte occurrences 1 is that constructor, 1 the SubagentStop input schema (@158554284), 2 are documentation strings, 7 are rewriters of an already-built payload and 1 is a packed constant table. No elicitation payload carries it, and transcript_path itself still names the top-level session.
claims.depends: The elicitation sidecar path is derived from the hook's session_id, so it always lands in the TOP-LEVEL session's sidecar dir (the <uuid>/ dir beside subagents/); csift merges it only when reading a top-level transcript (src/elicitation.rs), a subagent lane skips the read entirely, and a subagent's MCP elicitation surfaces under its parent - agent-blind by construction, which csift does not pretend otherwise. The served remote-call branch does not reach this: it fires only when an options bag carrying remoteCall is passed, which the three-argument elicitation builders cannot do, so the sidecar key stays a real session uuid rather than a served: string. If a future build moved the elicitation payload onto a per-lane path the way SubagentStop's agent_transcript_path already does, the sidecar would split across lanes and csift's top-level-only merge would miss it.
claims.instrument: Install a trivial PreToolUse hook that appends its stdin JSON to a file, run a tool from inside a subagent, and compare the recorded `session_id` with the subagent transcript's own basename: they must differ, `session_id` must equal the top-level uuid, and `agent_id` must name the subagent. Counting rule: one hook invocation per tool call.

claims.depends: csift's ghost-pending guard drops a sidecar-unresolved pending whose `csiftKey` appears STRUCTURALLY on a native record (as a `tool_use` block `id` or a `tool_result` `tool_use_id`; a key merely quoted in prose fails the block-id check), because the native transcript outranks the sidecar. Without it a rejected elicitation is reported pending forever by `list`, `search` and `status`, duplicated beside its own flushed native record. Cost is paid only when at least one AUQ/ExitPlanMode key is sidecar-unresolved: one mmap plus a per-key byte scan, parsing only the lines that contain the key bytes.
claims.instrument: With the elicitation hook installed, open a plan and REJECT it: `<uuid>/elicitations.jsonl` holds a `csiftPhase:"pending"` line with no matching `resolved` line, while the native transcript already carries that same key as a `tool_use` id (`csift show @<session> --uuid <the tool_use id>`), and `csift list @<session>` reports no pending elicitation. Counting rule: group sidecar lines by `csiftKey`, one group per elicitation. The unit test `native_closes_on_a_structural_tool_use_id` in src/elicitation.rs pins the structural check.

claims.behavior: In 2.1.258 a spawned lane's tool pool is built at ONE statement in the single agent runner - Kl=Pe?void 0:VE(e, ..., d,!1,cn,ga), Br=Kl?.resolvedTools??fe (@163776755) - and VE either passes the list through or applies the pool filter dAo (@163857126); dAo( has exactly two byte occurrences, its declaration and that single call, so nothing else can apply the exclusion set. The filter reads e.filter(C=>{if(zh(C))return!0; if(an(C,kc)&&f==="plan")return!0; if(ax(C,XNe))return!1; ...}) and closes with if(f==="plan"&&!v.some(C=>an(C,kc)))v.push(_6) (@163853640). The exclusion set XNe carries both tool-name constants - kc = ExitPlanMode and Ki = AskUserQuestion (@160046190) - so both are dropped from a pool built through the filter; but ExitPlanMode is RE-ADMITTED whenever the agent's own permissionMode is plan, and force-appended if the pool lacks it, while AskUserQuestion has no re-admit arm. An mcp__ tool is admitted before any exclusion is consulted: zh(e){return e.name?.startsWith("mcp__")||e.isMcp===!0} is the filter's FIRST branch (@162672568). Two paths bypass the filter entirely, so the exclusion is structural only for pools BUILT THROUGH it: the two main-thread agent pools call VE with the bypass flag true (@179223800, @180633380), and the runner's own useExactTools parameter short-circuits it, which the FORK arm of the Agent/Task spawn sets while passing the parent's tool list verbatim (availableTools:Ge?C.options.tools:Do, ...Ge&&{useExactTools:!0} @163921690, fork gate Ge @163910324); a second fork/hydration spawn does the same (@172859900), while the remaining two useExactTools sites pass lists already filtered through VE. The absence is nonetheless what the corpus shows: census 2026-09-04 over 8149 subagent transcripts (counting rule: one .jsonl under a subagents/ path component, journal.jsonl excluded; one record per matched tool_use block on a type:"assistant" record) finds 0 AskUserQuestion and 0 ExitPlanMode tool_use records, and 12 mcp__ tool_use records spread over 8 of those transcripts.
claims.depends: Keying the elicitation sidecar on the top-level session alone is sound only because the two invisible tool-shaped blockers do not occur in a subagent lane; a subagent's MCP elicitation is the one kind that can, and it surfaces under the parent session that owns the sidecar. csift leans on the measured absence, not on the filter being unconditional: a forked lane and a main-thread agent pool skip the filter, so a fork that inherited AskUserQuestion from its parent could in principle emit one, and its pending state would be invisible to csift - the sidecar is keyed on the parent while the tool_use would sit in the child transcript. AGENTS.md section 3.10 and SPEC.md section 6.10 should therefore say excluded from every agent pool BUILT THROUGH THE FILTER, with the fork and main-thread bypasses named, rather than main-thread-only.

claims.behavior: A session's sidecar directory (the `<uuid>/` dir beside the transcript, the same dir that holds `subagents/`) is created LAZILY: it does not exist at session start and appears only when something first writes into it, so an elicitation sidecar file is typically born mid-session, well after any watcher started.
claims.depends: `csift wait` re-attempts sidecar discovery on EVERY poll instead of only at start, and seeds a newly discovered file at baseline offset 0 because a file born after start is wholly post-start; the startup-only lookup meant a sidecar born mid-wait was never watched, so `--until auq` timed out while the final assessment said waiting-hitl.
claims.instrument: Run `csift wait @<uuid> --until auq --timeout 60 --interval 50` against a session that has no sidecar directory yet, then trigger the session's first AskUserQuestion: the condition must fire rather than time out. Counting rule: one discovery attempt per poll, one wait per ask. The e2e test `p10_wait_sees_a_sidecar_ask_that_lands_mid_wait` in tests/cli/live/wait.rs pins the mid-wait discovery.

checks.instrument: For every top-level transcript under ~/.claude/projects, compare stat -f %B on its sibling <uuid>/ directory and on that directory's elicitations.jsonl against the transcript's FIRST record timestamp (parsed from the jsonl, not from file metadata)
checks.observed: 64 top-level transcripts; 42 have a <uuid>/ sidecar directory; 20 have an elicitations.jsonl. Directory birth minus first-record timestamp: n=42, min +1s, median +3262s, max +1101283s - 42 of 42 strictly after the session's first record. Sidecar-file birth minus first-record timestamp: n=20, min +24s, median +98230s, max +1258058s - 20 of 20 strictly after. Not one directory and not one sidecar file existed at session start.
checks.rule: One measurement per top-level transcript that has a sibling directory named after its uuid. Session start = the timestamp of the first record in the transcript that carries one. Birth time = the APFS creation time from stat -f %B. 'Lazy' = birth strictly greater than session start.
checks.note: File birth times alone are not a safe instrument here - measured against the transcript FILE's birth time the same directories appear to predate it (median -148026s), because forked and copied transcripts carry record timestamps predating their own file. Anchoring on the first record's timestamp is what makes the rule sound, and under that rule the result is unanimous: 42/42 directories and 20/20 sidecar files were born after their session started, the median sidecar arriving more than a day in. That is exactly the condition the wait loop's per-poll rediscovery exists for. Both cited code sites are verbatim at the claimed lines (src/subagent/discover.rs 5-14, src/live/wait.rs 110-126), and the e2e test p10_wait_sees_a_sidecar_ask_that_lands_mid_wait exists at tests/cli/live/wait.rs:175.

claims.behavior: Claude Code hands a hook its payload as ONE JSON object on the hook process's STDIN. The keys a tool-shaped hook reads are `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id` and `transcript_path`; a tool elicitation additionally carries `tool_use_id`, and the two MCP elicitation events carry `elicitation_id` and `mcp_server_name` instead.
claims.depends: csift's elicitation-sidecar hook recipe parses exactly those keys: `hook_event_name` + `tool_name` pick the kind and phase, `tool_use_id` / `elicitation_id` / `mcp_server_name` build the `csiftKey` the merge pairs `pending` against `resolved` on, and `transcript_path` derives the sidecar path (with a `session_id` glob as fallback). A renamed key never errors - the script exits 0, the sidecar is never written, and `list`'s `sidecar_present` reads false, which is the honest "hook unknown, cannot conclude" arm rather than a wrong "nothing pending".

claims.behavior: Claude Code 2.1.258 constructs a type:"system" / subtype:"hook_response" message with exactly the fields hook_id, hook_name, hook_event, output, stdout, stderr, a conditional exit_code and outcome, in one function Th (@161999622), but (a) Th opens with if(!xSe(e.hookEvent))return; where xSe admits only var J2r=["SessionStart","Setup"] unless a session-wide allHookEventsEnabled flag is set (@161998723), and (b) it is NOT a transcript record: its sink is _u(e){Kr().enqueue(e)}, an in-memory bounded queue whose only two drains feed SDK and bridge message writers (@158424073). Its siblings hook_started and hook_progress open with the same gate and end at the same sink. The path that reaches it is the exit-status-0 outcome arm of the shell/command hook runner, which hands Th the finished hook's streams and, in the very next statement, yields an attachment instead (@165866018). Corpus census 2026-09-04: 0 records with type:"system" and subtype:"hook_response" across every transcript jsonl under the projects root.
claims.depends: csift's gated harness.meta.system leaf DOES classify such a record (verified against a synthetic fixture), but the record has no top-level content, so the leaf's [<subtype> <level>] <content> render produces [hook_response] with empty text: the hook's stdout/stderr are not matchable through it, and show --line shows the same empty excerpt. Only --raw would reach the bytes. And since no such record is ever written, csift cannot use it as evidence a hook ran. The on-disk trace of a hook that ran is the ATTACHMENT family instead, minted by the same outcome arms that feed the dropped hook_response (@165866018), stamped by Sn as {attachment, type:"attachment", uuid, timestamp} (@165765262) and appended by the recorder (@166105359). Corpus census 2026-09-04, counting one record per type:"attachment" line whose attachment.type begins with hook_: hook_success 364356 - csift leaf harness.meta.attachment, gated behind --attachments / --count-by attachment - carrying exactly command, content, durationMs, exitCode, hookEvent, hookName, stderr, stdout and toolUseID beside its type, on all 283417 sampled; hook_additional_context 88795 - csift leaf harness.meta.hook, gated behind --additional-context - when the hook injected context; then the smaller siblings hook_cancelled 770, hook_non_blocking_error 93, hook_blocking_error 30, hook_system_message 5 and hook_stopped_continuation 3. So "nothing at all otherwise" was wrong: a hook that ran and injected nothing still leaves a hook_success attachment.
claims.instrument: `csift search "" <target> -t harness.meta.system --count-by label` (the leaf is gated: without an explicit `-t` reaching it those lines are never parsed), then address one hit with `csift show <target> --line <n> --raw | jq 'keys, .subtype'`. claims.behavior: A hook's stdout `additionalContext` is injected ONLY when the returned JSON nests it under `hookSpecificOutput` together with a `hookEventName` matching the firing event; a bare top-level `additionalContext` is discarded, and Claude Code's own diagnostic for that shape is the literal `Did you mean hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (with a hookEventName)?`.
claims.depends: Dropping the `hookEventName` echo is not a fully silent no-op, and the two ways to get it wrong differ. Omitting the nesting entirely (a bare top-level `additionalContext`) is ignored WITH a logged diagnostic naming the fix. Nesting it but echoing the WRONG event name THROWS: `Hook returned incorrect event name: expected '<Event>' but got '<Event>'. Full stdout: ...`. Also, neither path records a `hook_response` transcript record - see ELI-020 - so the phrase 'still records its hook_response' should be struck.

claims.behavior: A hook matcher is consulted for 23 hook events, not two, and what it is tested against varies by event. The runtime switch _Xn (2.1.258 @165829264) returns tool_name for PreToolUse / PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure / PermissionRequest / PermissionDenied, command_name for UserPromptExpansion, source for SessionStart / ConfigChange / DirectoryAdded, trigger for Setup / PreCompact / PostCompact, a normalised to_model for PreModelSwitch / PostModelSwitch, notification_type for Notification, reason for SessionEnd, error for StopFailure, agent_type for SubagentStart / SubagentStop, load_reason for InstructionsLoaded, a path derivation for FileChanged, and - for the two MCP elicitation events - mcp_server_name. Three further events (TeammateIdle, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted) hit an explicit bare return;, so they have no matched field and the filter is skipped for them. Elicitation and ElicitationResult therefore DO take a matcher, and it selects which MCP server the hook fires for. 21 is a different number: it is the size of Wje, the LENIENT-GRAMMAR set (@165830254), which excludes StopFailure and FileChanged - both matched, both parsed with the strict grammar. The grammar is Cnr (@165828787): /^[a-zA-Z0-9_|, -]+$/ split on /[|,]/ with each part trimmed for a lenient event, /^[a-zA-Z0-9_|]+$/ split on | only otherwise. An absent or empty matcher matches everything, and so do * and .*, but by two different mechanisms: Kwt short-circuits on an empty matcher and on * (if(!n||n==="*")return!0, @165831574), whereas .* fails BOTH grammar character classes, so Cnr returns undefined and .* matches through the new RegExp(n) fallback further down that same function. Only SXn's reporting flag treats all three alike: ht=!je.matcher||je.matcher==="*"||je.matcher===".*" fed to matcherIsMatchAll (@165845802). An event whose matched field is undefined also always matches, because SXn's filter expression is v ? hooks.filter(h => !h.matcher || Kwt(v, ...)) : hooks (@165845284).
claims.depends: csift's registration recipe remains correct in practice for a different reason than stated: registering Elicitation and ElicitationResult with NO matcher matches every MCP server, which is what the SKILL.md recipe wants - a matcher would narrow it to one server and silently stop writing the sidecar for the rest. The claim that those events take no matcher at all is what is wrong. Two knock-on cautions for the recipe: because both elicitation events sit in the lenient set, a matcher containing a colon fails the character class, so Cnr returns undefined and Kwt falls through to new RegExp(n), where the colon is an ordinary literal - such a matcher still matches rather than disabling the hook, so the live check the old instrument proposed would not show what it expected; and a matcher of .* reaches the same regex fallback rather than the * short-circuit, with the same match-everything result.

claims.behavior: 10000 characters is a THRESHOLD, not a hard cap, and crossing it does not silently truncate. Every injected hook payload passes through ipe, which opens if(e.length<=o)return e; with {threshold:o=NQn} (2.1.258 @165809812) and NQn=1e4 (@160361495). Above the threshold the harness persists the payload to a tool-results/hook-<id>-<n>-<source> file beside the transcript and injects a <persisted-output> pointer carrying the true size and a preview ($3 writes the file, Npe renders the pointer, @160363597); only if persisting fails does it truncate, and then it appends [Hook <source> truncated at 10000 chars - persist-to-disk failed: <error>] (@165809932). claims.behavior: backupFileName is a key that is always emitted; only its VALUE is ever null, and a null has exactly two producers, both read verbatim in 2.1.258. The snapshot builder's missing-file branch writes {backupFileName:null, version, backupTime, realParentDir} when the tracked path cannot be stat'd at snapshot time, and it also fires the deleted-file telemetry counter and logs the path as missing (@162372460); the backup constructor's ENOENT catch returns the same null-name entry when the copy source cannot be stat'd (@162378288). Every other exit of that constructor either throws or returns a real store name. So a null means the tracked file did not exist when the snapshot was taken - not that a copy failed. A null entry is never carried forward: the reuse branch requires typeof backupFileName === 'string' (@162372836), so a null-name path is retried by the constructor at the next snapshot. The share of nulls is therefore a per-snapshot property of whichever paths are being tracked, and the corpus rate is a fact about this machine's editing history rather than about Claude Code. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one probe per (snapshot line, tracked path) entry with 'present' meaning a non-null value: 252,071 of 316,158 entries name a store file (79.7 percent) and 64,087 are null (20.3 percent), while the KEY backupFileName is present on 316,158 of 316,158. Earlier runs on the same growing corpus gave 78.4 percent (2026-09-02) and 78.5 percent (2026-09-03), and the 2026-09-02 per-session spread was 79 to 99 percent among sessions with at least 250 entries.

claims.behavior: The hint is emitted only when the Bash command matches a 19-alternative FORMATTER-IDIOM regex (--write, --fix, --in-place, --auto-correct, run format, run fix, (yarn|pnpm) format, lint:file, lint:fix, black, isort, ruff format, cargo (fmt|fix), rustfmt, go fmt, terraform fmt, dprint fmt, swiftformat, phpcbf), not after every write-shaped command; a command that fails that regex is never stat-checked at all, and a backgrounded Bash call is skipped outright. When it does fire, Claude Code stats every read-set entry and keeps those whose mtime moved past both the command start and the recorded read instant. The sentence uses a real pluralizer, so the literal is "N file" or "N files", never the literal "file(s)"; the named list caps at 5 comma-space separated paths with " and M more" for the rest; each path is rendered relative to the cwd with a fallback to the raw (absolute) path when relativization fails; and the closing clause interpolates the Read tool's registered name, so the tail is "Call <tool name> before editing.]" rather than a fixed string.
claims.depends: `recover` parses the hint into named paths plus the remainder count, resolves each against the CARRYING record's own `cwd`, and raises a hard `hint_modified` boundary - the one signal that attributes a formatter-class rewrite to concrete files. A target hidden in the truncated remainder is undetectable: a documented limit rather than a silent gap, and a change to the sentence head or the relative-path convention would remove csift's only authoritative formatter attribution.

claims.behavior: The attachment is built by walking the whole read set, skipping any entry recorded with an offset or limit (full-view reads only), requiring the file's mtime to have moved past the recorded read instant, requiring the content hash to differ, and requiring a non-empty rendered diff. It names the file in `filename` and carries the excerpt in `snippet`; `content` is the sibling edited_image_file payload's key, not an alternative spelling on the text form, and `filePath` does not appear at all in current data (0 of 1047 records). The 16 KB budget is the literal constant 16384 and is CUMULATIVE across one batch of attachments: attachments are filled in order until the running total of snippet lengths reaches 16384, after which every remaining snippet is replaced with the empty string. So an empty snippet is not a per-file overflow but a position-in-batch effect, and it is the degraded form of the same record rather than an empty edit.
claims.depends: `recover` reads it as an `ExternalEdit` HARD boundary and names the empty-snippet degraded form explicitly; reading an empty snippet as "no change" would silently continue a replay across an unseen external edit, and a payload key rename would drop the only content-bearing external-edit signal. The attachment cannot distinguish a human edit from a formatter run, which csift discloses.

Measured over 2,281 snapshot pairs (2026-09-02, one row per snapshot line after the first in its transcript, 'changed' meaning at least one tracked path's version differs from the previous snapshot line): the flag was NEVER true without a version change - (true,false) 0, (true,true) 586, (false,true) 1,278, (false,false) 417 - so a true flag implies a change while a false flag says nothing, and 1,278 real version changes carried false. The empty (true,false) cell is mechanical rather than statistical: the only producer of a true value was the file-history reducer's track case, which runs ONLY for a path absent from the newest snapshot and splices that new backup in before writing, so a true-flagged line always differs from its predecessor. Since 2.1.208 (buildDate 2026-07-13) the flag is uniformly false: that build replaced the track-case call to the snapshot writer with the literal true (2.1.207 @219311145) by the file-history-delta writer (2.1.208 @218963658), removing the only producer of a true value. In the audited 2.1.258 the snapshot-writer wrapper occurs exactly three times - the definition (@166123089) plus two call sites, the reducer's case 'snapshot' (@162369799) and the resume backup-copy (@162384622) - and both call sites pass the literal false, while the writer method itself passes its argument straight into {type, messageId, snapshot, isSnapshotUpdate} and appends it unchanged (@166106053); so no branch remains that can write the flag true. The build still READS it: a transcript-replay reducer collapses a snapshot flagged as an update onto the earlier line carrying the same messageId (@166147270). On disk, measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one value per raw file-history-snapshot line bucketed by the month of that line's snapshot.timestamp: 4,134 lines with true on 45 (2026-05), 299 (2026-06) and 242 (2026-07), and zero from 2026-08 onward (0 of 1,180 and 0 of 213). Joining each line's messageId to the record with that uuid in the same file gives no mixed cell: all 586 true-flagged lines name an ASSISTANT record with stop_reason tool_use at record versions 2.1.150 through 2.1.207, and all 3,540 resolved false-flagged lines name a user record (8 unresolved).
claims.depends: csift reads only `version` to detect a change and never consults the flag (no production `src/` reference to `isSnapshotUpdate` exists - verified 2026-09-04, it occurs only in unit-test and e2e fixture files), so its external-write instrument stays sound: a version JUMP is reported whether the flag rode true or false, and a flag-true snapshot with no version change reports nothing. Keying on the flag instead would not INVERT the detector, it would silently under-report - it would have missed the 1,278 changes that carried false against the 586 it would have caught, and it detects nothing at all on any transcript written by 2.1.208 or later, where the flag has no producer.

claims.behavior: `backupTime` records when Claude Code backed the file up, not when the file changed, so it is a bound on the write instant rather than the write instant. The backup never precedes the write (429 of 429 lags non-negative), but the size of the lag depends on which carrier records it: a newly tracked file's first backup rides a `file-history-delta` written at the moment of the write (146 measurements, median 0.25 s, max 3.20 s), while a later bump of an already tracked file waits for the next snapshot (283 measurements, min 29.9 s, median 1,409 s).

That path is invisible on disk: the key is stripped from the input both before the tool runs (@164149718) and before the tool_use is persisted (@164441203), and no persisted tool_use input in the corpus carries it (0 across 8,408 transcripts on 2026-09-04, counting one observation per tool_use block whose input object holds the key). checks.note: This is the strongest-confirmed claim of the five and the instrument sharpened it: the directional result (0 of 297 colliding blobs belonging to an EARLIER generation, 183 to the latest) means reading @vN by name is not merely unordered but systematically returns the newest generation's bytes, so the failure mode csift guards against is the one that actually occurs. The 120s tolerance is empirically the right size - 86.8% of agreements land inside 1s, so widening it would buy almost nothing while admitting collisions. claims.behavior: The two carriers of the partial-read banner are SUCCESSIVE, not concurrent, and neither current construction is pathless. Through 2.1.204 (buildDate 2026-07-07) the banner was injected into the rendered tool_result as "<system-reminder>[Truncated: PARTIAL view - showing lines 1-N of T total ...]" - pathless: read in the 2.1.204 build at @221262800, where both variants begin at "showing" with no filePath. ONE release changed the whole shape. At 2.1.205 (buildDate 2026-07-08; 2.1.204 is the last build with zero occurrences of the literal read_truncation_notice, and the two are adjacent releases) the carrier became a separate read_truncation_notice attachment whose banner always names the absolute path, the tool_result injection was deleted, AND the reconstruction-time sentence appeared - all in that same build: 2.1.205 carries the reconstruction builder at @224400100, which 2.1.204 does not have (the byte string "offset/limit to page through" occurs twice at 2.1.204, both inside the read-time construction, and four times at 2.1.205; read_truncation_notice occurs 0 times at 2.1.204 and 19 at 2.1.205). In the audited 2.1.258 the grammar reduces to one constant, "[Truncated: PARTIAL view - " (@160022476), and exactly two constructions, both path-bearing: the read-time one, "<abs path>: showing lines 1-N of T total (tokens, cap). Call Read with offset/limit for the next page ..." with a no-line-pagination variant "<abs path>: showing the first N of M characters ...; this file has very long lines and cannot be paginated by line ..." (@164912914, @164913177), pushed as {type:"read_truncation_notice", banner, toolUseID} (@164459799); and the reconstruction-time one, "<abs path>: showing N of T lines. Call Read with offset/limit to page through. ..." or "<abs path>: this view is incomplete and the file cannot be paginated by line. ..." (@165981354), injected into the reconstructed payload, guarded against double-application and never persisted. No pathless construction exists in 2.1.258; the pathless form survives only as a READER, two sites testing content.startsWith("<system-reminder>" + the constant) to recognise a partial view in a pre-2.1.205 transcript (@163598800, @165981354). At 2.1.259 the writer (@165285536), both notice-set readers (@164382016, @166794069) and the renderer (@166836572) survive while the two 2.1.258 sites that named the attachment type in a persistence gate are gone - the bisect records those two consumers being folded into a general attachment-persistence predicate - so the attachment-only reading holds there as well. Corpus re-measured 2026-09-04, one observation per banner occurrence, HEAD position meaning the text before the "[Truncated:" bracket is empty or exactly "<system-reminder>": 504 head-position tool_result copies, every one pathless and every one on a record whose version is 2.1.202 or lower, with zero head-position copies at any higher version; 207 attachment banners, all path-bearing and none pathless, earliest at 2.1.206; and zero head-position occurrences of the reconstruction sentence (its 16 raw occurrences today all sit mid-content, quoted inside ordinary tool payloads). Those 2.1.202 and 2.1.206 figures are CORPUS FLOORS, one release wide of the writer boundary, because this machine ran no 2.1.203, 2.1.204 or 2.1.205 build at all.
claims.depends: csift parses no banner text on any surface - re-verified 2026-09-04, a grep for 'PARTIAL view' or 'read_truncation_notice' over src/ and tests/ matches nothing - so all three grammars, the carrier migration and the path/pathless split are inert for it. Its partial-read instrument is the STRUCTURED read coordinates instead: toolUseResult.file and the file attachment supply startLine/numLines/totalLines, and push_read_event (src/recover/carriers.rs 178-181) classifies a Read as a FullSnapshot only when start_line == 1 && observed >= total && total > 0, else as a PartialRead. The exposure this claim guards is therefore not the banner wording but the absence of coordinates: a truncated view delivered with no numLines/totalLines falls back to total = observed and classifies FULL, so a partial view would be replayed as a complete file.

claims.behavior: The unchanged-file dedup has TWO branches, both gated by one lookup that returns undefined - and so disables both - under the tengu_read_dedup_killswitch gate, on a remote call, or when dedupUnchangedReads===false. Branch A (source:"seeded") fires when the remembered entry is startup-seeded, is NOT a partial view, and the NEW call asks for the whole file (offset===1 and limit===undefined); it compares the file's timestamp for exact equality with the remembered one. Branch B fires when the remembered entry is NOT a partial view AND itself carries a defined offset (i.e. it came from a windowed Read, not from an edit/write-seeded entry), the new call's offset and limit match the remembered ones exactly, and the file's timestamp is exactly equal to the remembered one. Both branches additionally require a pending-handover guard to be false. Because a whole-file Read stores offset===undefined, branch B never dedups a plain whole-file re-read.
claims.depends: The `!isPartialView` precondition is why a token-cap-truncated read is always re-read in full later, which is the only reason csift's contentless `file_unchanged` handling has not yet produced a wrong recovery.

claims.behavior: Claude Code strips a Write result of type update through stripForStorage, which rewrites the stored object to {...e, content:"", originalFile:null} unless one of TWO early returns fires: the content is already empty with an empty-or-absent originalFile, or the structuredPatch is an empty array with a null originalFile (the second guard is newer than 2.1.229). The strip is not applied at persist time to every result: it runs as a sweep over the message array that skips the most recent 200 messages (the interactive call site uses that default; the headless flush path passes a window of 0, stripping every eligible message). An update-type Write carrier can therefore land in the transcript with an EMPTY content string and no original content at all.
claims.depends: csift's carrier extractor treats any toolUseResult with a filePath and a content string but no oldString/newString as a full-snapshot anchor and calls buf.reset_to_full(content, ...). A stripped update carrier therefore resets the sparse reconstruction buffer to a zero-line file: reset_to_full clears the known-line map outright, so the prior content does not survive as explicit `??? lines A..B unknown` gaps - the total collapses too, and coverage reports 0/0 lines while --salvage reports no content seen at all.

code.snippet: buf.reset_to_full(content, *total_lines, e.line_no);

claims.behavior: An image block's `source` carries a kind field; every image block observed on disk is `base64` (payload in `data`) plus a `media_type`, and the raw line always carries the `"media_type"` key in its compact form. The `url` kind is an Anthropic-API source shape that Claude Code 2.1.258 never writes: 0 image references out of 2977 in this corpus use it, and the binary contains no `type:"url"` construction. csift keeps the kind verbatim and would report a url-sourced image as having no bytes to extract, but that arm is defensive rather than exercised.
claims.depends: csift selects candidate lines with an OR of three needles - the compact pair `"type":"image"`, the key-only `"media_type"`, and the bare value substring `base64` (src/image/refs.rs:96-98, combined by `.any()` at line 101). The serialization tolerance comes from the UNION: the pair needle alone would miss a line reserialized with whitespace around the colon, but the key-only and bare-value needles both survive it.

claims.behavior: Claude Code writes the model-facing image handle into the carrying record's own text as the literal marker `[Image #N]`, one marker per pasted image, and echoes the same handles as that record's `imagePasteIds` array. The marker is minted and inserted at PASTE time, not at submit: the image-paste keybinding hands the clipboard image to the paste callback (2.1.258 @181174777), whose image branch mints an id, stores the entry under it, and appends the template to the input text (@181171669), the template being the one-line function that returns `[Image #<id>]` (@162013342). At submit the record builder writes the submitted text block first and the image blocks after it on ONE user record, with the same ids in `imagePasteIds` (@169779566). Marker ORDER is not guaranteed to match block order: the block array and `imagePasteIds` are built in a single pass over the paste store's values, which is ascending by numeric id (@169787110), while the markers sit wherever the operator's editing left them in the input text, so the two orders can diverge. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per user record with a non-empty `imagePasteIds`: 659 records, 639 with the marker count equal to the image-block count AND the marker order equal to `imagePasteIds`, 18 with the same numbers in a DIFFERENT order (markers 179,181,180 against ids 179,180,181; markers 33-41,43,42 against ids 33-43; markers 3,4,9,2,19,22,23 against ids 2,3,4,9,19,22,23; markers 108,107 against ids 107,108), and 2 with mismatched counts. The harness's own reader is number-keyed, never positional: the inverse parser sitting immediately after the template maps each match to {id: parseInt(...)} (@162013342). A handle is unique within one prompt, but the counter does NOT restart at #1 on every prompt: the allocator starts at next = 1, mint() only ever does next++, and the advance helper raises next and never lowers it (@162027126), so within one process handles climb monotonically - measured across one transcript the distinct handles climb 1..624 over many prompts (2026-09-02) - and a fresh process starts at 1 again, which is what makes a handle non-unique within a transcript (IMG-006).
claims.depends: csift joins `#N` by NUMBER: when the record carries `imagePasteIds` covering every image block, image block k takes `imagePasteIds[k]` (the submit path writes the blocks and the array in one ascending-id pass); without the array the positional marker zip stays, and only when the marker count equals the image count (a mismatch leaves `seq` unset: a back-reference to a compressed-out image, never a misassignment). A `queued_command` attachment's prompt takes the same join. The handle feeds `csift image --id N` and the `[N images: #a #b]` annotations. What breaks if the fact moves: a build that wrote the image blocks in text order instead of id order would make the array join misassign; the corpus census of marker order against `imagePasteIds` is the instrument.
claims.instrument: `rg -o '\[Image #[0-9]+\]' <transcript> | sort | uniq -c` for the raw markers against `csift image @<session> --format json | jq -c '{handle, seq, line}'`. Counting rule: one marker per regex match, one row per content-deduped image.

claims.behavior: A transcript's [Image #N] handles are neither dense nor anchored at #1: the number comes from one per-session counter that is only ever raised, and a handle reaches a record only if its marker survives to submit. Re-measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root: 177 files carry [Image #N] handles; 100 of them start above #1 (9 of those top-level); 77 carry at least one hole inside their own [min, max] - the largest top-level file holds 575 distinct handles over #1..#624 with 49 holes, the next 120 over #1..#131 with 11 holes. The counter produces both shapes. The allocator returns next++ and never reissues or lowers a number, its advancePast only raises it, and startEpoch resets the minted set and never the counter (byte 162027126); on resume every handle in the LOADED history raises next before the session mints anything (byte 162027795), which is why a continued history starts above #1 - in the one top-level transcript headed by a compact_boundary the highest inherited marker is 619 and the first minted imagePasteIds are [620, 621] (re-checked 2026-09-04). The holes have named causes rather than 'inherited from paste time': one counter serves both marker templates, which sit side by side ([Pasted text #N] and [Image #N], byte 162013247); a large TEXT paste mints a number (byte 181170595 - only a paste over the size or line threshold mints, a small one is inserted verbatim) whose marker is replaced by the pasted content at submit and so never reaches a record (byte 162014339); and an image paste whose marker leaves the input before submit is deleted from the draft store with its number already spent (byte 170594396). The submit-time expansion is overwhelming but not absolute: 28 [Pasted text #N] markers survive corpus-wide across 8 files (2026-09-04).

claims.behavior: One pasted image can appear as several separate image blocks inside one transcript, and the traced cause is a RECALLED OR EDITED DRAFT resent under its existing paste ids. In 2.1.258 the path is: a turn-end user-cancel with an empty input restores the last user record into the draft (byte 181627085), and the explicit restore entry reaches the same function through setImmediate (byte 180779402); restoreMessageSync filters that record's image blocks out of its content and puts them back into the draft store keyed by the record's own imagePasteIds (byte 180778472); the paste-id helper keeps an id already minted this epoch instead of issuing a new one (its allowCurrentEpochSkip branch, byte 162029083), and the queued-message path re-adds queued images under their existing ids (byte 181689815); on the next submit the draft's image pastes are turned back into blocks and ids (byte 169786520) which the record builder writes, together with imagePasteIds, onto a NEW user record (byte 169779530). Neither cause this claim used to state survives its gates. There is no surviving store to re-send from: the draft's clear empties the whole paste map (byte 180837212), the submit handler calls it on every non-keybinding submit (bytes 181685480 and 181685514), the queue branch clears independently (byte 181580116), an input-change subscriber deletes every image paste whose marker has left the text (byte 181169506), and the submit chain forwards only pastes whose marker is still in the submitted text (byte 181576900). Compaction cannot carry an image either, and that closure is an enumeration rather than an absence: isCompactSummary:!0 has exactly five sites in this build (count re-run 2026-09-04) - three mints at 164805849, 164834441 and 164840504 whose content is the template string built at 164802880, and two re-readers at 169764319 and 180335298 that carry message verbatim and mint nothing. Magnitude, re-measured 2026-09-04 over the two largest image-carrying transcripts (one observation per image block reachable from a record's message.content, direct or nested in a tool_result array; distinct image = base64 length + 60-char head + 32-char tail): 1,146 blocks over 897 distinct images (191 repeated groups, 249 extra copies, most-repeated image 9 copies) and 239 blocks over 191 distinct (37 groups, 48 extra copies, max 4), so a raw block count over-reports the inventory by roughly a quarter, not by an order of magnitude. The corpus signature matches the traced cause: 229 of the larger transcript's extra copies sit on records csift labels user.unsent - superseded drafts of one message - and 171 of its 191 repeated groups have every copy under one parentUuid (35 of 37 in the smaller transcript). Corpus-wide the same day, all 235 isCompactSummary records carry string content, zero image blocks and no image media type. Two minority shapes stay unattributed: 8 groups with an isMeta copy (a file-attachment re-render) and a pasted image echoed back inside one turn by a tool result.

The keep-latest rule is unaffected by the correction, because a restored copy is resent under the SAME imagePasteIds and the newest occurrence therefore carries the same #N; and the head-AND-tail fingerprint stays load-bearing - fingerprinting on the base64 head alone collapsed 245 blocks into 170 groups on one transcript (2026-09-02), since same-dimension screenshots share a PNG prefix.

The Read descriptor registers a `stripForCreation` that removes `pages`, and only `pages`, and only when the result type is `parts` - `function kjn(e){if(typeof e!=="object"||e===null||e.type!=="parts"||e.pages===void 0)return e;let{pages:n,...r}=e;return r}` (164898866) - the result assembler applies it in a single statement before the record mint (164456451 into 164457235), and the 2.1.258 output schema states the rule verbatim: the page images are `Present only transiently in-process: the page image bytes are delivered solely as image blocks in the model-facing tool_result content and are not retained on the tool_use_result, so this key is absent on the emitted/persisted result` (164898052). That is a fact about the KEY, not about the bytes. The same assembler builds the model-facing content through the Read mapper's `parts` arm (164903101): when the in-process pages array is non-empty the tool_result content becomes an ARRAY of one text block plus one `{type:"image",source:{type:"base64",...}}` block per extracted page (or a text placeholder for a page that could not be processed), and when it is empty the content is the plain string `PDF pages extracted: N page(s) from <path>`. Both halves land on one record. The arrival of the image-block arm is a BINARY boundary, not the corpus floor the earlier text named: the mapper's per-page failure template, the pages strip predicate and the pages schema entry are all ABSENT at 2.1.240 and all PRESENT at 2.1.243, so the change landed in the window (2.1.240, 2.1.243]; closing it to adjacent releases needs the 2.1.241 and 2.1.242 builds, which are published but not cached here. The plain-string era therefore runs 2.1.196 through 2.1.231 as a CORPUS statement whose true upper bound in the binary is 2.1.240.

claims.behavior: Claude Code keeps a session registry under its home directory, one JSON row per live top-level session at `<claude-home>/sessions/<pid>.json`. The observed key set is `pid`, `sessionId`, `cwd`, `startedAt` (millisecond epoch), `procStart` (the owner process's creation instant), `version`, `kind`, `entrypoint`, `status`, `updatedAt` and `statusUpdatedAt`, plus row-dependent `peerProtocol`, `messagingSocketPath`, `name`, `nameSince`, `nameSource`, `peerFeatures`, `pidDomain`, `bridgeSessionId` and `tmux`. `kind` is a closed four-value set (`interactive` | `bg` | `daemon` | `daemon-worker`), of which only `interactive` occurs on an interactive host; `entrypoint` is NOT a closed pair - the writer copies `$CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` through verbatim and the reader accepts any string, so `cli` and `sdk-cli` are two members of an open set. The row is keyed on disk by pid, and the session it describes is named by the `sessionId` field, not by the file name.
claims.depends: `csift status` and `csift wait` join this row as one of three verdict surfaces, looking it up by scanning the directory for the matching `sessionId` and reading `pid`, `status`, `statusUpdatedAt`, `procStart` and `pidDomain`; a renamed key silently drops the registry leg out of the join and every verdict degrades to the no-registry lane.
claims.instrument: `python3 -c "import json,glob,pathlib;[print(sorted(json.load(open(p)))) for p in glob.glob(str(pathlib.Path.home()/'.claude/sessions/*.json'))]"` - every row prints a superset of {pid, sessionId, cwd, startedAt, procStart, version, kind, entrypoint, status, updatedAt, statusUpdatedAt}; then `csift status @<session> --format json | jq '.evidence[] | select(.surface=="registry")'` shows the row csift joined. Counting rule: one observation per `.json` file in that directory (non-`.json` sidecars excluded by extension), at one instant - the directory is current state, not history.

claims.behavior: The registry status `shell` is not a working state: the harness computes `idle` and then relabels it `shell` while a local background shell task is open, so `shell` means idle at end of turn WITH a background shell still running. `busy` is the only registry status that signals the session is doing work.

Reading `shell` as running - as csift did through v0.10.0 - makes an idle session with a dev server open never satisfy `wait --until stop`.

Counting rule: one status reading per known background-shell state (open, then closed), taken from a second session so the observed one stays idle.

claims.behavior: Each task file carries `{id, subject, description, status, blocks, blockedBy}` on every file, plus `activeForm` on most and occasionally `owner` or `metadata`; `blocks` and `blockedBy` are arrays. The ids are STRINGS on disk - a short all-digit ordinal of 1 to 3 characters, e.g. `"13"` - and the file name is that id by construction: the create path allocates `String(max+1)` (160151681) after scanning the list directory and parsing every `<digits>.json` stem for the maximum (160151347), then writes `{id, ...record}` pretty-printed at the id-named path (160152489, path builder 160149591). The `status` set is CLOSED, not open. The record schema pins it to exactly `["pending","in_progress","completed"]` - `var INe=m(()=>ee(["pending","in_progress","completed"])), He=m(()=>c({id:i(),subject:i(),description:i(),activeForm:i().optional(),owner:i().optional(),status:INe(),blocks:R(i()),blockedBy:R(i()),metadata:ge(i(),de()).optional()}))` (160146996) - and that schema is safeParsed on EVERY read, logging a validation failure and returning null (160152613), so a file carrying any other value is dropped by the harness itself. The fourth token `deleted` exists only on the TaskUpdate tool's INPUT schema, as `INe().or(x("deleted"))` (164400902), and it is a DELETE COMMAND rather than a status: the handler branches on it, calls the delete helper and RETURNS before the status assignment (164403078 into 160154941, which removes the file), so `deleted` is never persisted and no task file can be found carrying it - a deleted task's file does not survive on disk. Corpus census 2026-09-04 over both owner-directory forms under `<claude-home>/tasks/` (one observation per task `.json`): 424 files across 184 task directories, of which 28 hold task files; 0 unparseable; status completed 280, pending 114, in_progress 30 - exactly the three schema values and nothing else; ids 424/424 strings, all-digit, lengths 1 char x119, 2 chars x297, 3 chars x8; stem == id on 424/424; `blocks` and `blockedBy` arrays on 424/424; `activeForm` 337, `owner` 36, `metadata` 34.
claims.depends: csift treats anything that is not `completed` as an open row rendered with its VERBATIM status (in-progress rows first, then numeric id order, blockers named), and tolerates a bare-number STRING id. Under the closed enum that rule is still the right one and needs no widening: it is correct for the three persisted values, it survives a future fourth value without a code change, and it never has to model `deleted`, which cannot appear on disk. What would still break csift is a numeric-id assumption - parsing the id as a number, or deriving it from anything other than the file stem, which the allocator guarantees is the id - and rendering a status through a closed match instead of verbatim, which would drop rows the harness still considers open.

claims.behavior: The LIVE in-flight census under `<claude-home>/jobs/<short-id>/state.json` - `inFlight:{tasks, queued, kinds[], drainableMonitors?, wake?}` - is written only from a BACKGROUND process. Its writer opens with a two-condition early return, `async function bre(e,n){let r=a.CLAUDE_JOB_DIR;if(!r||a.CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KIND!=="bg")return;...}` (160491066): the process must own a job directory AND declare itself a background session. It is fed by the unattended-monitoring watch, which returns an empty teardown unless the same background predicate holds (180767309), and it reaches disk through the job-state writer (160481069) at the namespace builder's `job` case (157727146). The census has TWO producers, not one: beside that writer the classifier bridge emits `inFlight:BMe()` at six sites (176346170, 176346905, 176348460, 176349321, 176350134, 176357092) under the WIDER gate `function Qa(){return bt()||a_()!==null}` (158816923) plus the existence of a job record. In 2.1.258 that reduces to background-only, because `a_()` reads a `bgTakeover` field whose only setter has no call site: counted 2026-09-04, `setBgTakeover` has exactly two byte occurrences - a constant-table entry (76566868) and the method declaration (158813771) - and nothing assigns `bgTakeover` directly (its four occurrences are the constant table, the field initialiser, the setter body and the reader), so `a_()` is always null. The same two-occurrence shape holds in 2.1.257, 2.1.259 and 2.1.260. An INTERACTIVE session is excluded from the live CENSUS, not from the FILE: a session that launches or promotes a background job CREATES that job's record and seeds `inFlight:{tasks:0,queued:0,kinds:[]}` into it - the left-arrow path (180415596), the fleet-view resume picker (170633704) and the `taskFreeInFlight` launch option (180374171) fed by a command spawn (180379242) and a repl fork (186899839), all through the job-record creator (168068200) and its record constructor (160497478) into the same state writer, none of them env-gated - and non-background processes also write terminal states into an existing record (160501145; the `claude stop <id>` CLI clears `inFlight` to `void 0` at 168096464). That seed describes the CHILD job at birth, not the launcher's own tasks. The load-bearing consequence therefore survives: no on-disk file states how many background tasks an INTERACTIVE session currently has armed.
