claims.behavior: On unix hosts the registry's `procStart` is the owner process's creation instant rendered as an asctime-like string in the C locale and in UTC (`Sun Aug 16 09:04:23 2026`). The row writer stamps it unconditionally - `N=S({pid:process.pid,sessionId:Q(),cwd:ye(),startedAt:Date.now(),procStart:await ja(process.pid),...})` (158819054) - and that helper (158135801) delegates to a runner that executes `ps` with `["-o","lstart=","-p",String(e)]` and `env:{...,LC_ALL:"C",TZ:"UTC"}` (158136222); the synchronous twin carries the same command as one shell string, `LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p ${e}` (158134674). A bare `ps -o lstart=` names the SAME instant in the machine's local zone AND in the machine's locale, so the two strings can differ in FIELD ORDER as well as in offset: measured 2026-09-04 on a UTC+10 host, 4 of 4 live rows gave a 0.0 s residual once the registry value was parsed as UTC and the bare `ps` value as local, while the raw strings differed by the full 10 hours and by field order (registry `Thu Sep 3 00:16:07 2026` against bare `ps` `Thu 3 Sep 10:16:07 2026`) - which is what the C-locale pinning buys: a fixed parse format. The Windows FILETIME (100-nanosecond ticks since 1601-01-01) is carried in a SEPARATE string key `procStartFt`, and three facts about that pair are readable here: the platform helper returns exactly one of the two keys (`function OU(e){return c()?{procStart:void 0,procStartFt:e}:{procStart:e,procStartFt:void 0}}`, 158135690), the platform reader REFUSES a `procStart` value on the FILETIME platform (158135600), the row parser accepts both keys (159697157) and consumers read `procStartFt ?? procStart` (159693134). Which key a Windows registry ROW actually carries is UNDETERMINED from this binary: the row writer never calls that helper, and all seven occurrences of the helper name are its definition (158135699) plus six call sites - the messaging-auth key file (158809990, 158810361), a pid-probe record (162121127), a worktree lock reason (163535163), a background-job record (167589560) and a job-holder record (168563787) - none of them the row writer. The audited bundle is a per-platform darwin build (`DD_SOURCEMAP_GROUP:"darwin"`, 156312375) whose platform predicate is constant-folded to `function c(){return!1}` (158132377), so the Windows arm of both the helper and the ps runner is dead code here rather than absent, and no FILETIME producer exists in this build to read.
claims.depends: csift reads `procStartFt` first and falls back to `procStart` (src/live/registry.rs:76), mirroring the harness's own `procStartFt ?? procStart`, and its parser accepts either rendering off whichever key answered: an all-digit string is read as a FILETIME, anything else as an asctime instant in UTC (`parse_registry_proc_start`). It then compares INSTANTS against the local `ps` value with a 2-second tolerance for its pid-reuse guard; comparing the two as strings or as same-zone values flags pid reuse on every row and turns every live session into a stale-dead verdict. Because csift consults both keys, it is safe under either answer to the undetermined Windows-key question. Two further consequences of the C-locale pinning: csift's fixed `%a %b %e %H:%M:%S %Y` parse works on the registry value precisely because the harness pins the locale, and a bare local `ps` string must never be substituted for it - on this host the unpinned rendering is day-before-month and the fixed format would not parse it. When either side is absent or unparseable csift degrades to a pid-only probe and discloses that the reuse guard was skipped.
claims.instrument: For one live session read `procStart` from its `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` and run `ps -p <pid> -o lstart=`: the two strings differ by exactly the machine's UTC offset while naming one instant. Counting rule: one paired reading per live pid, and seconds between the two parsed instants after zone assignment (expect 2 or fewer); agreement in a UTC+0 zone is evidence of nothing, so run it where the offset is non-zero. The unit test `registry_proc_start_parses_as_utc` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs pins the parse side.

claims.behavior: The `ps -p PID -o lstart=` form used to probe pid liveness is not universally available on unix: busybox `ps` (Alpine and similar) rejects `-p` and `lstart` outright and fails for a LIVE pid exactly as for a dead one, while `/proc/<pid>` answers liveness directly on Linux and does not exist on macOS, where the `ps` form is reliable.
claims.depends: csift falls back to a `/proc/<pid>` directory test when the `ps` form fails, keeps the no-such-process verdict only when that is absent too, and discloses the skipped reuse guard; without the fallback `status` read a live session as stale-dead on musl hosts, which the release matrix's musl lanes caught.
claims.instrument: In a busybox container run `ps -p 1 -o lstart=` (non-zero exit or empty output) beside `test -d /proc/1` (succeeds), then `csift status` for a live session there must not report stale-dead and must name the reuse guard as skipped. Counting rule: one probe outcome per platform family (busybox, glibc Linux, macOS); only a real run on a busybox host exercises the fallback. The unit tests `probe_pid_own_process_guard_states` and `probe_pid_reports_a_reaped_pid_dead` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs pin the alive and dead arms.

claims.behavior: `ps -o lstart=` renders its date in two field orders - `Sun Aug 16 09:04:23 2026` (%a %b %e) and `Sun 16 Aug 09:04:23 2026` (%a %e %b) - but the discriminator is the ps implementation together with LC_TIME, not the host family. A single macOS host emits both: C and en_US give month-first, en_AU and en_GB give day-first. glibc procps-ng emits month-first in every locale tried, so it contributes only one order. Both orders reach csift in production: on a machine whose LC_TIME is day-first the default probe returns the second order and the pid-reuse guard still matches.
claims.depends: csift tries both patterns before giving up and degrading to a disclosed pid-only probe; matching only one order silently disables the pid-reuse guard on the other family of hosts, which shows up as an `alive (pid only)` evidence value rather than as an error.

claims.behavior: A registry row outlives the process it describes: SIGKILL writes no closing transition, so the file stays on disk carrying its last `status` and `statusUpdatedAt` while its pid names nothing. It is NOT kept until it is replaced, though - any peer session may run the registry sweep, which deletes every `<pid>.json` whose pid is dead (and reports `Prior session exited uncleanly` for interactive rows). Measured removal latency after a SIGKILL ranged from under 200 ms to still-present 35 minutes later on the same machine, so a stale row is a race won or lost, never a guarantee.
claims.depends: the owner-pid probe is the only thing that retires a stale row: csift ranks a dead or reused pid above every other surface and reports stale-dead, naming whether the tail was mid-tool or settled when the process ended; trusting the row alone would report long-dead sessions as running.

claims.behavior: Claude Code ships an atomic-write helper that writes through a temporary file and a rename, plus a documented non-atomic fallback whose error is prefixed `atomic write failed first: `. Both paths are present in the shipped binary. But the binary DOES attribute one of the four JSON sidecars a reader joins: the session-registry row `<claude-home>/sessions/<pid>.json` is written with plain `fs/promises.writeFile` on both its registration and its update path (and the sibling `.fleetview-heartbeat` likewise), NOT through the atomic helper - the writing module's own import header binds `writeFile as Mg` alongside the `join` and `readFile` aliases that same function uses. A plain writeFile truncates in place, so the registry row is not merely 'to be assumed' observable half-written: it is positively established as such, and csift's skip-on-unparseable guard is required rather than merely prudent. The other three sidecars - subagent `meta.json`, workflow run manifests, harness task files - remain unattributed by this instrument; a serialized write chain (`pidFileWriteChain`) orders the registry row's writers against each other but does nothing for a concurrent external reader.
claims.depends: csift reads all four sidecars as a whole-file read plus a parse and silently skips a file that fails either step, so one caught mid-write yields a DOWNGRADED answer with no disclosure: `status` falls back to its no-registry lane, a task row disappears from the tasks section, and a subagent loses its type and its teammate discrimination. Retrying the read once, or disclosing the skip as evidence, is the only way that failure could become visible.
claims.instrument: `strings -n 40` over the installed Claude Code binary grepped for `atomic write failed first` shows the helper (temp file, symlink-refusing O_EXCL open, fsync, rename) and its in-place fallback; `strings -n 12 <binary> | grep -oE 'appendFileSync|renameSync|mkdtempSync' | sort | uniq -c` gives 24 / 15 / 11 and bounds call sites from above without attributing any. To ATTRIBUTE a sidecar, do not count - resolve the alias: find the writer by a literal only it contains (for the registry row, ``Ct(e1(),`${process.pid}.json`)``), then find the nearest preceding `import{...}from"fs/promises"` header in the same module text and require that every identifier the writer calls is bound there. The registry row resolves to plain `writeFile`. A live race (poll `~/.claude/sessions/*.json` at high frequency and count reads that fail to parse) can corroborate but must report its denominator: a 90-second 5ms poll here made 13414 listings and 93898 reads yet saw 0 row mtime changes, so its 0 parse failures prove nothing - a race with no write in the window is unqualified.

claims.depends: csift's `CHILD_RECENT_SECS = 300` is set from that distribution, and a child lane is `generating` only on the CONJUNCTION tail-record age <= 300 s AND last assistant `stop_reason != end_turn`; the retired 15 s window read a lane mid-generation as settled 1 time in 17 (under-counting `live_count`, so `waiting-children` collapsed to `idle-eot`), and the mtime-based `active` state is gone.
claims.instrument: Over a corpus of `subagents/agent-*.jsonl`, compute consecutive record timestamp deltas inside each file and the age of each file's tail record, then take percentiles. Counting rule: one gap per adjacent timestamped-record pair WITHIN one file (lanes with fewer than two timestamped records excluded), one age per lane; gap percentiles pooled over gaps, age percentiles over lanes. Age is always measured from the tail RECORD timestamp, never file mtime. The unit test `children_report_generating_needs_recency_and_no_end_turn` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs pins the conjunct.

claims.behavior: Most DEAD subagent lanes do not end at an end_turn. Re-measured 2026-09-04 (one observation per lane, taken from that lane's newest assistant record; dead = newest timestamped record more than 1 h old; 1 MB tail window): of 7,900 lane transcripts 7,889 are dead and 7,884 carry an assistant record inside that window (5 do not) - tool_use 3,243, end_turn 1,988, null 1,995, stop_sequence 658 - so 5,896 of 7,884 (74.8%) carry a stop_reason other than end_turn, and a rule keyed on stop_reason alone would report nearly three quarters of them as still running (earlier passes read 73.4% on 2026-09-02 and 74.3% on 2026-09-03, on smaller corpora). Two of the four buckets are not API values. null is a record drained before its message ended: the assistant record is built at content_block_stop from the still-partial message (byte 165442985) and the API stop_reason is back-patched onto every already-yielded record only when the message_delta arrives (bytes 165444595 and 165444727). stop_sequence is harness-minted rather than an API stop: it is the hardcoded value of the synthetic error-record builder (byte 165933431, whose record literal at byte 165934091 carries stop_reason "stop_sequence", an empty stop_sequence, null stop_details and an all-zero usage), and all 658 such dead-lane tails carry exactly that fingerprint plus isApiErrorMessage true, in two message key sets (591 without a diagnostics key, 67 with). Their leading text is not the identifying instrument: today the 658 split exhaustively into 501 that open with a limit line (480 session, 21 weekly) and 157 that open with an API Error string. On the runner's own death path nothing is appended after a lane dies: the runner span holds exactly four transcript-append call sites, all before the abort throw (byte 163789156), and the finally teardown is 17 named registry- or memory-only stages (byte 163789418, the stage names re-read 2026-09-04), none of which can write a record. That scope is the runner's own path only - a settled lane can still gain a LATER isMeta user record when a queued completion pulse is delivered to it (the lane-selection claim), which never changes the newest ASSISTANT record this claim measures.
claims.depends: tail-record recency is therefore the load-bearing conjunct of csift's generating state - the <= 300 s age test is what keeps those roughly three quarters of dead lanes classified settled (src/live/children.rs), since stop_reason alone would mark them live. The stop_sequence bucket is the sharpest case: those tails look like a model stop and are in fact harness-minted API-error records, so no csift surface may read stop_sequence as evidence that a lane finished cleanly.

claims.behavior: A MAIN transcript GROWS while its session is idle - queue enqueues, `attachment` records and metadata lines are appended with no model turn - so file mtime or byte growth alone is never evidence of activity.
claims.depends: csift classifies WHAT landed rather than whether the file moved: `tail_shape` reads record shape and ignores mtime, and `wait` folds each newly appended record through `classify` instead of treating growth as an event; an mtime-based liveness heuristic would call every idle main session running.

code.snippet:
//! F9: growth alone is never activity - a main transcript grows while idle (enqueues,
//! attachments). This module classifies WHAT the tail is, not whether the file moved.

claims.instrument: Leave a session idle and enqueue a message, or let another session's background task complete into it: the file grows (`stat` mtime and byte length advance) while `csift status @<session> --format json | jq .verdict` stays idle. Counting rule: compare the byte delta over a fixed idle interval against the verdict, then `csift search '' @<session> --turn -1 --count-by label` to show no new agent records.

All 56 sites that enqueue `mode:"task-notification"` in 2.1.258 were enumerated (the count re-verified 2026-09-04 by a whole-binary grep of that literal): 48 take the lane from `Ze()` (47 carry the literal `agentId:Ze()`; one is a module constant with no `agentId` whose only use spreads `agentId:Ze()`), 4 are caller-parameterized with a `Ze()` default - `agentId:v??Ze()`, so a task launched by a subagent notifies that subagent's lane, and the backgrounded-shell completion pulse addresses itself inline this way at 164968716 - 2 take the lane from the owner-liveness selector `function eVe({ownerAgentId:e,keepaliveReason:n,delivering:r,taskRegistry:o}){...return _&&e?uo(e):Ze()}` (164954861), which returns the owner agent's lane while that owner task is registered and running (or backgrounded with live children) and `Ze()` otherwise, and 2 address the owner agent with no liveness test at all. `Ze()` is not a root constant: `function Ze(){let e=g()?.sessionId;if(e)return uo(e);let t=n();return t.identity.mainAgentId(t.id)}` (156787676, over `function g(){let e=C();return e?.session?void 0:e}` at 156787544) resolves the CURRENT lane - the installed agent context's session id when there is one, the main agent id otherwise - so `agentId:Ze()` reaches the main lane exactly when its callback runs with no agent context installed. The owner-liveness selector is reached from exactly three call sites: the agent-completion enqueuer (164953647), the workflow completion pulse (168826340) and the agent-resume notice (175694140). Receipt with its counting rule, re-grepped 2026-09-04: the CALL form `eVe(` occurs exactly 4 times - those three plus the definition at 164954870 - while a boundary-anchored grep of the bare identifier returns 13, the other nine being two constant-table entries (73315983, 79883560), one export list (166239124), two import lists (168822034, 175676643) and four occurrences of an unrelated view component's local variable (180400142, 180402607, 180402871, 180402915). Delivery is a SECOND gate: the per-lane queue fold `function t9e(e,{isMainThread:n,currentAgentId:r})` (162030912) first drops slash-command entries (`if(Run(f))return!1`), then on the main thread admits `fg(f)` (`agentId === Ze()`) and inside a child admits ONLY items of mode `task-notification` whose `agentId` equals that child - so a child branch exists by construction. On the main lane the queued item becomes a prompt record through the REPL drain (181584368); on a child lane the wake router resumes the addressed agent with the pulse as its prompt, `promptOrigin:{kind:"task-notification"}` and `promptIsMeta:!0` (179256653), the record is built `isMeta` with that origin (175692385), and the runner appends only that new record to the lane file (163784699). A delivered child pulse does NOT open with the raw tag: the task-notification case routes through the wrapper `sbt` (166046409 into 160018067), which prepends a `[SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT USER INPUT]` preamble constant measuring exactly 494 characters (counted 2026-09-04 from the literal at 160017550). Main-only delivery is therefore a corpus OUTCOME and not a routing rule: censused 2026-09-04 over 8,237 transcripts under the projects root (journal.jsonl excluded; one observation per `type:"user"` record whose message text starts with the raw tag OR starts with the preamble AND contains the tag), 2,895 deliveries in 25 main transcripts, every one with the tag at index 0, against 9 deliveries in 4 subagent lanes, every one `isMeta` true, `isSidechain` true, origin kind `task-notification` and the tag at index 494 - 8 written by build 2.1.252 and 1 by the audited 2.1.258. Other carriers of the same tag, counted separately and excluded: 8,324 `queue-operation` lines, 5,131 attachments, 1,819 non-opening user records and 883 assistant prose.
claims.depends: csift's child-lane state machine may legitimately use recency (the `generating` state) while the main-lane verdict never does - but the reason is not that a child transcript grows only from its own message flow: a child lane can gain a record it did not write whenever a pulse is addressed to it, and because that delivery RESUMES the lane, recency still tracks liveness there. The prose that needs correcting is the module comment at src/live/children.rs:8-10, which justifies child recency with 'notifications land in MAIN only'; the state machine itself needs no change. Any counting rule, in csift or in this ledger, that looks for a delivered pulse must not test for a raw `<task-notification>` opener: a child delivery sits 494 characters behind the system-notification preamble, and the raw-tag-opener rule is exactly what produced the earlier 'never in a subagent transcript' reading. Measured 2026-09-04 against the installed csift 0.10.3, the audited build's child-lane delivery is not merely mis-counted but invisible: an explicit `show --line` address on that record bails with `no such record(s)`, and a whole-lane `--count-by label` census lists no `harness.notification` key at all, because the record is `isMeta` and its tag is not at a section boundary. The main-lane trap that keeps recency out of the main verdict is unchanged.

claims.behavior: Each workflow run's `journal.jsonl` (one per `wf_*` directory) is written INCREMENTALLY - `{type:"started", agentId}` at spawn and `{type:"result", agentId, result}` at return - so for a RUNNING run `started` minus `result` is the number of that run's agents in flight (measured live: 57 started, 49 returned, 8 in flight). It is not a liveness test on its own: a killed, failed or abandoned agent never writes a `result`, so the imbalance is permanent - 613 of the 621 unbalanced entries in this corpus belong to journals untouched for 15 h to 77 days. The journal also carries a third type, `failed`, which is neither counted.
claims.depends: csift's `children_report` sums that difference across a session's journals as `journal_in_flight`; an imbalance is a LIVE signal precisely because a terminal dump would always balance.

code.snippet:
// Workflow journals: started - result per wf dir (incremental, so an imbalance is a
    // LIVE signal - a terminal dump would always balance).

claims.instrument: `rg -o '"type":"(started|result)"' <a wf_*/journal.jsonl> | sort | uniq -c`. Counting rule: one event per journal line, per type; started minus result equals the agents in flight for that run.

checks.instrument: `find ~/.claude/projects -path '*/subagents/workflows/*' -name journal.jsonl -print0 | xargs -0 cat` piped to a python type/key-set census; then per journal `rg -c '"type":"started"'` minus `rg -c '"type":"result"'` paired with `stat -f %m` age; then `csift status @<8-char prefix of a long-idle session> --format json`; then the file listing of the one workflow directory whose journal was written in the last hour.
checks.observed: 160 journals, 12,754 lines: `started` 6,687, `result` 6,066, `failed` 1. Exactly two key sets: {agentId, key, type} 6,688 and {agentId, key, result, type} 6,066. Corpus-wide started minus result = 621. 124 journals balance at 0; 36 carry a positive imbalance, and 35 of those 36 - 613 of the 621 - were last written 15 h to 1,843 h ago (77 days). `csift status` on a session whose tail record is 58 d 19 h old prints evidence `children: 3513 lane(s), 359 live (359 workflow agent(s) in flight)` and verdict `waiting-children`. The single journal written within the hour, belonging to a run that was actually executing, reads started 57 / result 49.
checks.rule: One event per journal line, per `type`; started minus result per journal directory. A journal counts as stale when its file mtime is more than 1 h old.
checks.note: The mechanism holds and was confirmed live, but the inference 'an imbalance is a LIVE signal precisely because a terminal dump would always balance' is refuted: 98.7% of the corpus-wide imbalance sits in long-dead runs. The consequence is a live csift defect, reproducible in one command - `csift status` on a session whose newest record is 58 days old reports 359 workflow agents in flight and returns the verdict `waiting-children`. src/live/children.rs:104-105 and 126-130 match verbatim; the `_ => {}` arm at 129 is what drops the `failed` type, so a failed agent inflates `journal_in_flight` by one forever. A fix would need to age the journal (or its run) the way child lanes are aged, and to count `failed` as terminal.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded call is never an in-flight call on disk: a `Bash` tool_use with `input.run_in_background:true` is answered by its own `tool_result` (`Command running in background with ID: ...`) as soon as the task is registered - measured at 56 ms on a live launch, and never pending in 3423 backgrounded tool_use records corpus-wide (0 pending, 0 orphan). Record-to-record the pairing reads as a median of 0.46 s for a shell and 0.37 s for an async spawn (main lane, one project dir), 86% of shells within 1 s and a tail out to 9.9 s, because the assistant record's own flush latency is inside that difference. claims.behavior: Claude Code appends whole LINES to a transcript through a single path, so complete-line framing is the guard a reader needs. The write queue turns each entry into one JSON-serialized line, accumulates lines into a chunk with a 100 MiB ceiling (MAX_CHUNK_BYTES 104857600) on a 100 ms flush timer (byte 166082942), and hands each chunk to appendToFile, which calls the one append helper with THREE arguments (byte 166085326) - so the helper's onlyIfExists parameter is undefined on this path and the ordinary append is either the storage backend's own append or a single appendFile(path, chunk, {mode:0600}) with a mkdir-and-retry fallback (byte 166117719, the direct arm at 166118675). A record larger than the chunk ceiling is not split by the harness: the drain flushes what it has and the oversized entry gets a chunk of its own, still one append call. The foreign-transcript appender, which writes in an explicit loop and can report a torn result (byte 166118748), is reached only under onlyIfExists, whose three producers in this build all target ANOTHER session's file. Claude Code models a torn tail rather than assuming it away: while a seal is pending the next append is prefixed with a newline (the head of the append helper), and a synchronous sealer opens the file write-only and append-only and writes a bare newline when the file is non-empty (byte 166084862) - so a torn line is fenced off, not completed. Measured (2026-09-02): no transcript was left with an unterminated final line (0 of 430 files) and no line was left unparseable (0 malformed in 20,677 lines censused by csift stats). A partially written final line is possible rather than routine - the longest single line was 2,609,260 bytes and 142 lines exceeded 64 KiB - but it was never caught: 0 torn tails in 18,238,418 samples covering 190 observed appends.
claims.depends: csift's tail reader and wait's incremental cursor both stop at the last newline and hold the torn remainder for the next poll; parsing the torn line would surface a spurious malformed-line count on every live read. The writer's own seal is a second reason to hold rather than to guess: a sealed tail is terminated by the newline the writer prepends to its next append, so the held remainder becomes a complete but truncated line, which csift's malformed-line accounting would then count out loud rather than hide - the honest outcome, and one no observation in this corpus has produced.
claims.instrument: Poll a live transcript's byte length in a tight loop and check whether the final byte is a newline: a torn tail appears transiently. Counting rule: one sample per poll. The unit test `tail_shape_reads_pairing_stop_reason_and_holds_torn_tails` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs asserts the torn line is neither parsed nor counted.

That is not a refutation - the polling loop resolves a file about every 14 microseconds when watching one file and about every 3.5 ms when watching 56, so a single-syscall append of a few-KB record can slip entirely between two samples, and on macOS a write(2) to a regular file is serialized against concurrent reads, which would make the window zero for any record the runtime emits in one call. claims.behavior: The shared <session-uuid>/ directory beside a transcript is minted LAZILY by the first write under it - in practice the first subagent lane append - and not by any elicitation. The path resolver keeps a top-level session transcript FLAT and puts only lanes, journals and session journals under <sessionId>/ (byte 157719971), so nothing addresses the directory until one of those is written; a lane write reaches it through the sidechain record path (bytes 166114240 and 166107661: a sidechain record carrying an agentId is enqueued against the lane path); and the directory is created only as a side effect of the append failing - the direct appendFile arm's catch does a recursive mkdir at mode 0700 and retries (byte 166118593; when the storage pin routes the append through the backend arm instead, that catch is not the arm that runs). Corpus consequence, re-measured 2026-09-04: 64 session directories, 27 of them holding subagents/, 20 holding the elicitation sidecar file; of those 20, 13 sit in a directory older than the file by more than 1 s (min 183 s, median 118,410 s or about 1.4 days, max 775,906 s or about 9 days) and 11 of those 13 also hold subagents/, while 7 have a directory born with the file. The sidecar FILE itself is not a Claude Code behavior at all: the shipped binary contains zero occurrences of the sidecar filename and zero of either marker field (re-confirmed on 2.1.258), because a recording hook writes that file.
claims.depends: csift wait re-attempts sidecar path resolution on every poll instead of resolving once at start, and joins the file at offset 0 when it appears (wholly post-start by construction); a one-shot resolution would miss every elicitation that began after the watch, which is exactly the class of event a wait exists to catch. The directory may already exist when the watch starts - any session that has spawned a subagent has one - or may be born mid-wait, and csift resolves the path on dir.is_dir() alone, so the path can resolve long before any ask has occurred, at which point the sidecar file simply does not exist yet: absence at start is the normal state and never an error.
claims.instrument: With the elicitation hook recipe installed, watch a session with `csift wait @<id> --timeout 120 --format json` and let it raise an AskUserQuestion: the sidecar file beside the session's `subagents/` directory does not exist before that ask and does from it, and the pending marker lands in the wait census. Counting rule: one observation per elicitation - the sidecar file's existence before versus after the first pending ask; a session that never elicits never grows one.

A bare-string-only reader returns nothing on real data.

claims.behavior: Claude Code exports `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` into every Bash tool environment and its value is exactly the calling session's jsonl basename - but it names the TOP-LEVEL session in EVERY lane, including inside an in-process subagent, whose own id is withheld from the Bash env and handed only to hooks.
claims.depends: `csift whoami` uses this variable and nothing else (never a process-tree walk, never most-recent-mtime, which is a false-positive trap under concurrent sessions), refuses to guess when it is absent, reports `is_subagent`/`parent_session_id`/`depth` as null in the env form, and prints a lane note on every `@main` resolution; a subagent must use `@trap:<marker>` to name itself.

code.snippet: const SESSION_ID_ENV: &str = "CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID";

claims.instrument: In a Bash call run `echo $CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` and `ls ~/.claude/projects/*/$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID.jsonl` - expect exactly one file; `csift whoami` with the variable unset must error with guidance rather than pick a session. From a SUBAGENT's Bash call the same echo prints the parent uuid, while `csift whoami @trap:<a fresh marker>` prints the subagent's own ancestry chain - only a live subagent can show the divergence.

checks.instrument: Run from inside a live SUBAGENT's Bash call: echo ${CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID:+yes}   ;   ls ~/.claude/projects/*/$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID.jsonl | wc -l   ;   ls ~/.claude/projects/*/*/subagents/**/*$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID* | wc -l   ;   env | rg -c '<this subagent's own hex id>'   ;   csift whoami --format json   ;   csift whoami @trap:QuietAmberFalcon7412   ;   env -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID -u CODEX_COMPANION_SESSION_ID csift whoami
checks.observed: The variable was SET inside a subagent lane and its value resolved to exactly 1 top-level ~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<uuid>.jsonl and 0 files under any subagents/ directory - i.e. it named the TOP-LEVEL session, not the running lane. No environment variable in that same Bash environment contained the subagent's own id (grep count 0 over the full env). csift whoami --format json returned is_subagent null, parent_session_id null, depth null, and printed on stderr: 'csift: note: resolved via env ($CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID), which names the TOP-LEVEL session in every lane - from a subagent this is the PARENT's id, not yours. Lane fields are null under env-only resolution'. The text form printed 'lane  unknown from env alone (a subagent sees its parent's id here)'. csift whoami @trap:<a fresh 3-CamelCase-word + 4-digit marker> resolved on the FIRST try to the subagent's own transcript under <parent-uuid>/subagents/workflows/wf_*/agent-<hex>.jsonl and printed the ancestry chain 'subagent <hex> <- you (subagent, depth 0)' over 'session <parent uuid> ^ top-level root'. claims.behavior: Claude Code serializes every transcript line with the engine's own JSON encoder: the write queue turns each entry into JSON.stringify(entry) plus a newline (byte 156850169) and nothing between the entry object and the file re-encodes or unescapes it (the drain's serializer selection, byte 166086450). The escape policy is therefore exactly that encoder's - quote and backslash are escaped, and every code unit below 0x20 becomes a short escape or a \uXXXX form - so a rendered text can differ byte-for-byte from the raw line wherever whitespace or an escapable character sits. DEL (0x7f) is NOT in that set and reaches the line raw. Corpus census 2026-09-04 (one observation per jsonl line under the projects root): 49 lines in 25 files carry at least one raw DEL byte, and 0 lines carry any other raw control byte below 0x20.
claims.depends: csift derives search prefilter needles NECESSITY-ONLY and applies a per-needle safety predicate (whitespace-free, JSON-escape-free, at least 3 bytes), plus a marker list for the small closed set of render paths that fabricate text not present verbatim in the raw line; a needle failing the predicate would silently drop real matches, which is the one place the no-silent-truncation contract actually bites. csift's escape-worthy set (src/search/matcher.rs) counts DEL as escapable, which is a conservative SUPERSET of the encoder's real set: on the 49 corpus lines that carry a raw DEL it forgoes a prefilter needle it could have used, and it never drops a match, so the correction costs a fast path and changes no result.

claims.behavior: The COMPACTION shrink of a transcript is a RENAME over the path, not an in-place truncate: performCompactTranscript (166098791) writes a filtered copy to a sibling `<path>.compact.tmp.<hex>` and never opens the original for writing, then renames the temp over the live path (`await Ti(f,e)` at 166100780; Ti at 157575160 is a retry wrapper whose default operation is rename from fs/promises). A reader that already mmapped the old inode therefore keeps reading it intact, which is why the fixed-at-open contract survives compaction; the rename is additionally guarded by an inode-and-size re-check immediately before it, aborting with tengu_transcript_compact_failed if either moved, so a concurrent writer cannot be clobbered. The path is effectively unreachable by default: all three production entries (insertMessageChain arming a compact right after appending a compaction boundary at 166105640, the CCR v2 hydration delta at 166138449, and the write-queue drain backstop at 166087327) are gated on the store flag localGcEnabled, a class field defaulting to false (166076591), and performCompactTranscript additionally returns below a 5,242,880-byte floor; the ungated wrapper exported as compactTranscriptForTesting has no production caller. A storage-v5 twin, performCompactTranscriptV5, is taken when a storage object is present; this claim covers the filesystem path only. The rename statement must NOT be generalised to transcripts as such. A SECOND path shrinks the SAME inode in place: performRemoveByUuid (166095622) opens the transcript r+ and calls `await f.truncate(...)` before rewriting the tail, it carries no localGcEnabled test (removeMessageByUuid at 166095481 enqueues it unconditionally), and its trigger is the REPL stream's onTombstone handler at 181621337. That truncate is the in-place shrink that does exist; the compaction rename is the one that does not.
claims.depends: csift mmaps each transcript once (the single audited mmap site, src/parse/lines.rs) and reads it as a fixed snapshot; the compaction rename leaves that snapshot valid, while the ungated tombstone truncate can shrink the mapped inode under it, and no csift surface detects a shrink today (MISC-020 carries the reader consequence for `wait`). On a partly-written tail csift skips a BLANK final fragment uncounted (line_payload rejects an all-whitespace remainder, skipped_lines stays 0) but does NOT skip a torn one: a `{`-framed partial record is counted as ONE malformed line (skipped_lines 1) - disclosed rather than hidden, and stable across repeated runs at exit 0. That is the correct behaviour under the no-silent-truncation contract, but it is counting, not skipping.
claims.instrument: Run `csift search '' @main` repeatedly against the currently-writing session while it works; every run must exit 0 with a stable `skipped_lines` count. Counting rule: `skipped_lines` from the JSON summary across repeated runs.

claims.behavior: A transcript is normally EXTENDED by appends, but appends are not the only thing that reaches the file: one write queue and one 100 ms flush timer carry three item kinds, and two of them mutate a transcript in place (byte 166086064, the drain's item routing - only the third arm is an append). One in-place path is gated off: the compaction rewrite is enqueued only through requestCompact, which returns unless the store's local GC flag is set (byte 166084451), and that flag is a class field defaulting to false (byte 166076591). The version-stable handle for the gate is its env-and-gate pair, CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC falling back to a default-false feature gate (byte 179052977), not the field name: measured over the cached build ladder on 2026-09-04, the compaction rewrite and that pair are absent at 2.1.216 and present from 2.1.219 (2.1.217 and 2.1.218 are not cached), while the field name localGcEnabled appears only from 2.1.227 - at 2.1.219 and 2.1.226 the identical gate reads `requestCompact(e){if(!<module-scope flag>)return;this.enqueueCompact(e),this.scheduleDrain()}` over the same predicate, so the rename is not the feature's birth, and every build carrying the rewrite defaults it off. The other in-place path is NOT gated: a tombstone removal opens the transcript r+, truncates it at the removed record's line and rewrites the tail (byte 166095622), its live entries are ordinary REPL stream handlers (the tombstone handler at byte 181621337 and the refusal-continuation retraction at byte 181619649), and the selecting condition fires the disk removal exactly when the tombstoned record's index sits BELOW the append frontier - that is, when the record is already on disk (byte 179092749). When the uuid is not inside the tail window the same function falls back to reading, filtering and rewriting the WHOLE file, unless the file exceeds 52,428,800 bytes, where it logs that it is skipping the tombstone removal and gives up (byte 166096191, the ceiling constant at byte 166066127) - so a watcher's exposure depends on file size. That removal path and its ceiling log are present in every cached build from 2.1.191 through 2.1.259 (measured 2026-09-04), so the shrink half is at least that old - a floor, not a proof of absence before it. A live transcript can therefore shrink in place, and a byte-offset cursor can outlive the bytes it named. What does hold is the other half of the old sentence: the harness offers a watcher no event stream at all, only the file - the drain fires its in-process mirror callbacks on the append branch alone (byte 166086139), and the append arm writes only at the end of the file, with no seek and no rewrite (byte 166118593) - so content already on disk before a watcher's snapshot is never re-emitted to it; a 150 s sampler over 33 actively written transcripts (495 observations, 2026-09-03) saw 122 growths, 0 shrinks and 0 changes to any byte below the first snapshot's length, a growth-only window that cannot stand in for the missing gate. The user-facing rewind gesture is not a counter-example: a live trial on 2026-09-04 against build 2.1.259 took a transcript from 60 to 68 lines with no shrink and one branch point, so restoring a conversation forks logically by appending rather than truncating.
claims.depends: csift treats a transcript as append-only for LINE NUMBERS and byte offsets (a `show --line N` address, a `search` hit's `L<n>`, a `wait` baseline) and discloses when that premise fails: since v0.10.4 the readers that run repeatedly against a LIVE transcript - `wait`'s per-poll increment and the `status`/`wait` tail window - use plain positional reads (`parse::read_range`/`read_tail`), never a memory map, because a page of a mapped file touched past a new, shorter end faults with SIGBUS and no Result catches it; `wait` detects a shrink between two polls (the file is shorter than its baseline), moves the baseline to the new end and reports `transcript shrank N time(s) (lane: -bytes)` in its activity line and JSON `shrinks`. The one-shot full scans (`search`, `stats`, the `status` background scan) keep the memory map of SPEC 7a, whose sub-second life bounds the exposure. Before 0.10.4 `wait` mapped the whole file on every poll and skipped a shrunk file silently.

claims.behavior: The shipped binary's process start-time guard degrades to a PASS when its probe returns nothing. One probe is one shelled command, LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p <pid> with a 1 s timeout, returning the trimmed stdout or undefined on any failure or empty output (byte 158134674; an async twin at byte 158136222 has the same shape behind a cache that records a miss but never substitutes a value). Both guard forms then read a missing token as a MATCH - the guard returns true when the stored token is undefined, and the comparator returns true when either side is undefined (bytes 158134798 and 158134903) - so a pid whose start time cannot be read is treated as the same process rather than failing closed, and a consumer such as the delayed SIGKILL proceeds on that reading (byte 158133164). No in-process liveness probe substitutes for it, and that is an enumeration rather than an assumption: the same module exports a kill(pid,0) probe, a /proc/<pid>/stat reader, an ESRCH form and a /proc entry counter, and composes them elsewhere into a layered dead_pid | procstart_mismatch | zombie | live verdict, but none of the four is consulted on the start-time path. The environment fact that motivates the guard - a minimal (busybox) userland's ps rejects the -p flag and does not know lstart, so the probe fails even for a LIVE pid, while /proc/<pid> answers liveness directly on Linux and does not exist on macOS - is produced by the operating system's own process lister rather than by this binary, and belongs in its own specimen-only entry.
claims.depends: csift makes the same degradation VISIBLE instead of silent: its probe treats a failing or empty ps as no-verdict rather than dead, falls back to a /proc/<pid> directory test before declaring a pid dead, and when either side's procStart is missing or unparseable it reports the process alive with the reuse guard marked skipped and says so in the evidence (src/live/registry.rs) - a wrong Dead here turns every verdict into stale-dead. The binary's tolerance is why the fallback has to exist, and the disclosure is what separates csift's reading from the binary's silent pass.
claims.instrument: Run `ps -p $$ -o lstart=` on a busybox userland (empty output, non-zero status) versus on macOS or glibc Linux (a local-zone date). Counting rule: one probe per platform. The unit tests `probe_pid_own_process_guard_states` and `probe_pid_reports_a_reaped_pid_dead` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs pin the alive and dead arms; only a real run on a busybox host can confirm the fallback path.

claims.behavior: `ps -o lstart=` has exactly one format in the platform process-status utility - the started column's only format is a bare `%c` - so the rendering is whatever the caller's LC_TIME date-and-time entry expands `%c` to: both the FIELD ORDER and the weekday and month names follow the locale, not the host family. Measured on one macOS host on 2026-09-04 against one live pid: C and en_US.UTF-8 both give `Fri Sep  4 11:58:02 2026` (month first), en_GB.UTF-8 and en_AU.UTF-8 both give `Fri  4 Sep 11:58:02 2026` (day first), de_DE.UTF-8 gives `Fr  4 Sep 11:58:02 2026` and fr_FR.UTF-8 gives `Ven  4 sep 11:58:02 2026` - four renderings from one machine, two of them with non-English weekday names and one with a lowercase month. Claude Code removes the ambiguity for its own registry field by PINNING the environment: the session registration stamps `procStart: await ja(process.pid)` (byte 158819100), ja delegates to the async probe at byte 158136390, which spawns ps with `env:{...,LC_ALL:'C',TZ:'UTC'}`, and the sync twin Eie (byte 158134612) shells the same pin as a string, `LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p <pid>` (a third lstart probe beside them, at byte 158136613, pins the same pair and parses the result as UTC). A stored procStart is therefore always the C-locale order rendered in UTC, whatever the user's locale, and a probe that inherits the caller's locale sees whichever of the four that locale selects. The harness's own reuse guard fails open in the same direction as csift's: wAt (byte 158134798) returns true when the stored token is undefined, so an unavailable or unparseable probe never declares reuse.
claims.depends: csift's `ps_probe` (src/live/registry.rs) runs `ps -p <pid> -o lstart=` with the caller's inherited environment and tries exactly two strftime patterns, `%a %b %e %H:%M:%S %Y` then `%a %e %b %H:%M:%S %Y`, before falling through to `PsProbe::Alive(None)`. That covers the two English orders and nothing else, so on a host whose locale renders a non-English weekday the pid-reuse guard is skipped: measured today at csift 0.10.3 against one live registry row, the `pid` evidence row reads `alive (start-time guard matched)` under C and en_GB.UTF-8 and degrades to `alive (pid only)` under both de_DE.UTF-8 and fr_FR.UTF-8. The degradation is disclosed in the evidence row but its cause is not, and the reuse guard is off for that whole family of hosts. Pinning `LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC` on csift's own ps call, the way the harness does for procStart, would reduce the tolerated set to one pattern and close the hole.
claims.instrument: `for L in C en_US.UTF-8 en_GB.UTF-8 en_AU.UTF-8; do LC_ALL=$L ps -p <pid> -o lstart=; done` on a single host, then the same four locales around `csift status @<id> --format json | jq '.evidence[]|select(.surface=="pid").value'`. Counting rule: one rendering per locale; every order must yield `alive (start-time guard matched)`, because a strftime parse that falls through both patterns degrades to `alive (pid only)` and silently disables the pid-reuse guard.

claims.behavior: Claude Code accepts a `--fork-session` flag (registered at byte 170221888: 'When resuming, create a new session ID instead of reusing the original (use with --resume or --continue)'). It does NOT write a `forkSession` record field: the sentence 'forkSession follows across the compaction break. Distinct from the session-file chain parent (which is the post-compact summary). Absent from older producers.' is the `.describe()` text of a schema field named `logical_parent_uuid` (byte 158628227) - it documents the backpointer the fork OPERATION follows, and `forkSession` there is the operation's name. The fork validators require `sessionId` to be a UUID and, when supplied, `upToMessageId` to be a UUID (byte 177242904; the file-backed SDK twin words the same pair as 'not a UUID'). Corpus scan 2026-09-04, counting the quoted JSON key `"forkSession"`: 0 of 8,237 .jsonl transcripts (68 of them top-level), consistent with no such record field existing. A fork leaves NO trace in the origin file. The record that does exist there is a background HAND-OFF marker: `{"type":"continued-in","timestamp":...,"sessionId":<origin>,"continuedInSessionId":<successor>}` is minted by a single template (MYn at byte 160428091, exactly those four keys in that order) and appended to the PARENT transcript by a single writer (Eqe at byte 180375802, via `{onlyIfExists:true}` so it never creates the origin file, with a warn-level log on failure), under one gate inside the background spawner: `if(!Pe?.keepParent&&...)` at byte 180375167. The two callers that leave keepParent unset are hand-offs - the exit-dialog / background-this-session entry exported as forkSessionToBackground (byte 180378528, via 'command') and the REPL left-arrow / open-agents entry (byte 180414748, via 'left_arrow') - while the /fork path (byte 186899783) is the ONLY caller passing `keepParent:!0`, so the gate is false and nothing is written into the origin; neither SDK forkSession implementation touches the origin either. The two are easily confused because both spawn the child with `--resume <path> --fork-session` and because the hand-off entry is publicly named forkSessionToBackground. The reader side agrees: the resume driver (byte 163213541) drops a session from the resume picker and reports it running in the background precisely when its transcript carries continuedInSessionId, and skips that check when --fork-session is set. Corpus 2026-09-04: exactly 1 transcript carries exactly 1 continued-in record, whose sessionId equals the origin file's own basename and whose successor id resolves to a sibling transcript in the same project directory; a fleet bisection records continuedInSessionId absent at 2.1.248/250/251/252 and present at 2.1.257, which is why the corpus count is 1. The fork facts themselves - forkSessionId, forkParentSessionId, forkSourceAlive, forkBoundaryAt - are persisted only in the session and job registry (schema at byte 160477775, seed write at byte 168071855), never in a transcript.
claims.depends: csift models the compaction-fork CLONE (a byte-copied head whose first timestamped record is a `compact_boundary`, joined to its origin by that boundary uuid - `session::clone_head_boundary`) but not `forkSession`, and it has no `continued-in` leaf. On the transcript surface a fork is still indistinguishable from an ordinary resume, because the distinguishing state lives in the session and job registry, which csift does not read for lineage - so a consumer cannot tell them apart, and `list` surfaces no fork relationship. What csift genuinely lacks that transcripts DO carry is the `continued-in` record: modelling it would surface a background HAND-OFF (this session was continued in that one), not a fork.

claims.behavior: A tool-call record's only STRUCTURAL appearance of the tool NAME on the raw jsonl line is the `name` field of its `tool_use` block: measured over one project dir, 7764 of 7974 single-tool_use assistant records (97.4%) contain the name exactly once, the remainder being incidental content matches. The name is NOT mirrored on the result side - only 678 of 7986 single-tool_result carriers (8.5%) contain the tool name at all, so a result carrier is reachable only via the tolerant user-role matcher, not via a name needle. A tool whose name shares no substring with a scanner's needle set therefore leaves its tool_use line unreachable before any parse happens.
claims.depends: `csift files`' pre-JSON prefilter admits a line on exactly six needles - `Edit`, `Write`, `Bash`, `filePath`, `file-history-snapshot`, `is_error` - plus the tolerant user-role matcher; a renamed or new mutating tool whose name contains none of those and whose input key is neither `filePath` nor an error carrier is rejected pre-parse, so its mutations never reach the extraction step and never reach the malformed or dropped counters either.

claims.behavior: Since at least Claude Code 2.1.170 the API can return a SECOND `thinking` block inside one assistant message: a short summary of the reasoning beside it, in the conversation's language rather than a fixed user language (inside one session whose human writes Chinese, narration blocks appeared in both Chinese and English). It is identical in shape to a reasoning block - measured over the whole live corpus on 2026-09-04, all 111,390 thinking blocks (108,181 reasoning-tagged, 3,173 narration-tagged, 36 unsigned) carry exactly the block key-set {type, thinking, signature} with zero variation - so nothing on the wire separates the two except that signature's contents. Presence is NOT monotone in client version: it is a server-side behavior, and long runs of later clients wrote none. Per writing version on 2026-09-04: 2.1.170 wrote 61 narration blocks of 213 signatures, the earliest at 2026-06-10T02:10:12Z; the older clients present in the corpus (2.1.150, 2.1.156, 2.1.159) wrote 0 of 2,877; 2.1.177 wrote 0 of 3,842 and 2.1.191 0 of 10,030; 2.1.196 resumed; 2.1.258 wrote 208 of 5,027. The CLIENT-side classifier ships at 2.1.240, not 2.1.241: measured across the cached build ladder on 2026-09-04, isNarrationTaggedBlock and narration_classifier_error are both absent at 2.1.236, 2.1.237, 2.1.238 and 2.1.239 and present from 2.1.240, and AssistantNarrationSummaryMessage goes from 0 occurrences at 2.1.239 to 2 at 2.1.240 (2.1.241 and 2.1.242 are not in the cache, so the floor is bracketed by 2.1.239 absent / 2.1.240 present rather than walked build by build). Two further boundaries the old sentence hid: the render hint word is `(summarized)` from 2.1.240 through 2.1.247 and bare `summarized` only from 2.1.248; and the SUMMARY predicate is feature-flag gated for that whole stretch - isNarrationSummaryBlock reads `isNarrationTaggedBlock(block) && isSableThrushEnabled()`, where the flag is the env CLAUDE_CODE_SABLE_THRUSH falling back to a default-false gate, at 2.1.240 and still at 2.1.250, and becomes unconditional (`!!block.thinking?.trim() && isNarrationTaggedBlock(block)`) from 2.1.251, with the flag literal gone from 2.1.251 onward and from the audited 2.1.258. In 2.1.258 the classifier is a WeakMap-memoized pure predicate that decodes the signature and tests equality against the single constant `narration` (byte 176601862), and the message renderer branches on it to hand the block to AssistantNarrationSummaryMessage under the hint prop (byte 180070851); neither runs on the persist path.
claims.depends: csift splits the leaf `agent.thinking.narration` off `agent.thinking`; without the split an API-issued summary is counted as the model's own reasoning in every `search -t`, `--count-by label` and `stats` figure, and `verbatim` would replay it as reasoning. It is also the first leaf whose dotted path another leaf prefixes, which is why `-t` selection matches by dot SEGMENT (`-t agent.thinking` selects both leaves). csift classifies from the block's own signature, so none of the client-version boundaries above changes what csift reads: a narration block written by a pre-classifier client is still tagged in its signature and still classifies.
claims.instrument: `csift stats <target> --format json | tail -1 | jq '{narration_blocks, unknown_thinking_tags}'` counts narration BLOCKS per model; cross-check the leaf split with `csift search '' @<session> --count-by label | rg 'agent\.thinking'`, which on one measured session read 609 `agent.thinking` and 313 `agent.thinking.narration`.

claims.behavior: The tag separating the two thinking-block kinds is encoded inside the base64 `signature` at protobuf field path 2 -> 1 -> 8, taking the LAST length-delimited (wire type 2) field at each level; the payload decodes to the UTF-8 string `narration` or `thinking`.
claims.depends: `thinking_signature_tag` mirrors exactly that walk and `thinking_block_class` maps a decoded `narration` to `agent.thinking.narration` and every other outcome to `agent.thinking`. The LAST-field rule matches the client byte for byte, but on this corpus it is not yet load-bearing: a FIRST-field walk returned the identical tag on all 91,904 signatures (0 divergences), so today the two rules are indistinguishable from the data and only the client decoder decides which is correct. A shifted field PATH does break the decode. Every failure path - absent or empty signature, bad base64, truncated varint, unknown wire type, non-UTF-8 - degrades to untagged rather than erroring, in both the client (`default:return!1`, `catch{return}`) and csift.
claims.instrument: Take a signature from any thinking block (`csift show @<session> --line <n> --raw | jq -r '.message.content[] | select(.type=="thinking") | .signature'`), base64-decode it, then walk field 2, then field 1, then field 8, taking the LAST length-delimited field at each level; the payload is the UTF-8 string `narration` or `thinking`. Counting rule: one decode per thinking block, tag read from that block's own signature. The csift unit tests under src/model/tests pin the LAST-field rule and the full degradation matrix with hand-emitted protobuf fixtures.

claims.behavior: Narration-tagged thinking blocks do occur in subagent transcripts, but are orders of magnitude rarer there than in top-level ones. Measured 2026-09-03: 24 narration records in 5 of 7,780 subagent transcripts (0.06% of files) against 3,140 in 22 of 67 top-level transcripts (33% of files); a second pass hours later counted 7,799 subagent files, so the file total is live and only the order of magnitude is stable. All 24 subagent records sit under a SINGLE parent session and all carry client version 2.1.251; that session has 15 subagent lanes on one model id and only 5 of them carry any narration (per file 1/2/2/6/13), four with bare-hex subagent ids and one with a name-embedded teammate id. Nothing in the shipped binary decides whether a returned block is tagged: the tag bytes are copied verbatim off the stream (Hs.signature=Cu.signature, 165442020) and the only narration-aware client branch is a memoized read-only predicate (176601820) whose consumers touch no persistence, so the rate has no producer here and stays a measured base rate over a dated corpus. A lane-shaped thinking gate does exist, but on the REQUEST side and not over block tags: the subagent lane runner builds the child lane's config through sor (163781898 -> 158520661), which forces display:omitted for a synchronous, non-forwarding, non-exact-tools child lane and returns the parent config unchanged whenever the session is interactive; the value it may rewrite comes from the showThinkingSummaries setting through mEt/rAn (158520075), the settings schema declares that display as exactly summarized|omitted on both thinking-config variants (158538648), and it reaches the wire as the request's thinking parameter (165412140, spread into the request body at 165415790). Whether display=summarized is what makes a returned block carry the tag is decided upstream of this binary, and which display each lane actually requested is unrecoverable from disk: a byte census on 2026-09-03 found 0 records carrying a structured display, thinkingConfig or interactivity field (the bare tokens occur only as prose inside sessions that discuss them).
claims.depends: csift runs the identical signature classifier on every transcript it reads, subagent files included, so the rarity is a property of the data rather than a scope gap: the subagent-resident narration records are counted with no code change, and on any spanning surface the spanned-minus-restricted difference is exactly the subagent-resident count (24 on 2026-09-03: 3,164 spanned against 3,140 restricted). The client corroborates that the classifier sees everything the harness wrote - no client branch drops or reshapes a narration block before it is persisted. The adjacent fact that a subagent lane's records reach subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl by lane routing alone, with no block-type inspection on the write path, belongs to its own claim and is not this claim's producer.

claims.behavior: Claude Code derives the `<ENCODED>` project-directory basename from the session's canonical start cwd by NFC-normalizing it and replacing every UTF-16 CODE UNIT outside [A-Za-z0-9] with exactly one `-`, position-preserving: no collapsing of consecutive dashes and no case folding, so `.`, `/`, `_` and space each become one dash, an NFD-spelled accent recomposes to a single unit (one dash), and an astral character (two surrogate units) yields TWO dashes. Since 2.1.234 this is the DEFAULT rather than the only path: the basename is `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME ?? sanitize(cwd)`, and the override is honored only when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is also set and the value matches /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/ and is not a Windows reserved device name.
claims.depends: `path::encode_cwd` reproduces the transform unit-wise to locate the project directory; a char-wise or byte-wise replacement diverges on any non-ASCII cwd, so every subcommand that takes a real path or `.` as its target silently scans the wrong project or none.
claims.instrument: Pick any directory under `~/.claude/projects/`, read the `cwd` of the first record of one contained `*.jsonl` (`head -1 <file> | jq -r .cwd`) and apply the transform by hand: the result must equal the directory basename character for character. Counting rule: one output dash per UTF-16 code unit that is not ASCII-alphanumeric, so an astral character contributes two dashes and an NFC-composed accent one. The unit test `encode_matches_cc_exactly_on_non_ascii_and_windows_paths` pins NFC/NFD parity, the astral double dash and the Windows shape; to re-derive from the harness, run `strings` over the shipped Claude Code binary and grep for the literal replacement regex `[^a-zA-Z0-9]` and for `normalize("NFC")`, expecting one sanitizer and no case fold.

claims.behavior: Because the sanitizer does no slash, colon or case pre-processing, a Windows cwd encodes to a LETTER-led directory name - `C:\Users\x` becomes `C--Users-x` (the drive letter passes through, the `:` and each `\` are one unit each) - while a UNC root `\\server\share` becomes the double-dash-led `--server-share`; a Unix cwd is always single-dash-led.
claims.depends: csift's `@`-token grammar admits both encoded shapes: a leading `-` token and the `<letter>--...` drive shape are project-dir tokens (a drive-shaped token that matches no directory falls through to real-path resolution, since it can also be a relative path), and a UNC-encoded directory is targeted as `@--server-...` because a bare `--`-leading token is reserved for the mistyped-flag guard; without the drive-shape arm a Windows project directory is unreachable.

code.snippet:
#[test]
fn encoded_token_shapes_unix_windows_unc() {
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("-Users-dev-example-project"));
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("C--Users-dev-proj")); // Windows drive shape
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("--server-share-proj")); // UNC (leads with --)
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("Users-dev")); // no encoded lead-in
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("C--Users/dev")); // a separator disqualifies
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("C-Users-dev")); // one dash after the drive ≠ `C:\`

Counting rule: one dash per non-alphanumeric UTF-16 unit, so `C:\` yields `C--`. claims.behavior: Claude Code caps the encoded project-directory basename at 200 characters (`MAX_SANITIZED_LENGTH`) and stores anything longer as `<first-200>-<hash>`, so for a deeply-nested project the full encoding of the cwd does not exist on disk at all.
claims.depends: csift compares the encoded length against the same 200-character cap before falling back to the prefix scan; a wrong cap leaves every deeply-nested project unresolvable by `csift list .` and by every other path-taking target.

code.snippet: pub(crate) const MAX_SANITIZED_LENGTH: usize = 200;

claims.behavior: The cwd-to-directory map is many-to-one and Claude Code does not disambiguate collisions for any cwd of 200 encoded characters or fewer: two different cwds that encode identically share ONE projects directory, distinguishable only by the session uuid and by each record's own `cwd` field.
claims.depends: csift uses the encoded directory as the lookup key exactly as the harness does, and intends to keep, for a REAL-path target, only the files whose recorded cwd IS that path while an EXPLICIT encoded-dir token skips the filter. As of Claude Code 2.1.258 that filter no longer fires on real data: the harness now writes a session-state cache line as physical line 1 of every transcript, and read_first_cwd inspects only line 1, so the stored cwd reads as absent and every candidate is admitted under the absent-cwd keep. The mechanism is intact and testable only where line 1 carries cwd.
claims.instrument: `csift list <ENCODED-dir> --format json | jq -r 'select(.kind=="session") | .cwd' | sort -u` - more than one distinct value proves a collision inside that directory, and the same query against the REAL path must return exactly one. Counting rule: distinct `cwd` strings across the directory's top-level session rows.

checks.observed: Many-to-one confirmed constructively: two distinct cwds differing only in one separator character encode to the identical 112-character basename (equality check printed True) and share one directory. Guard behaves as documented WHEN the cwd is on line 1: the encoded-dir token returned 2 session rows (no filter, the user named the directory) while each real path returned 1. But the guard is inert against real transcripts: 0 of 66 top-level transcripts in the live corpus carry a cwd field on physical line 1 - line 1 is a session-state cache line in every case (62 'last-prompt', 3 'ai-title', 1 'queue-operation') - and csift's read_first_cwd (src/path/project_dirs.rs:109) reads ONLY the first line, so it returns None and the file is kept unconditionally. Demonstrated on a live directory holding 7 top-level transcripts of which 3 record a cwd that does not encode to the basename: both the encoded-dir token and the real path returned 7 rows; the real path should have returned 4.
checks.rule: A collision is two DISTINCT cwd strings whose encodings are equal - not merely two distinct cwd values in one directory, which the deep-cd case also produces. Guard efficacy = rows returned for a real-path target divided by rows returned for the encoded-dir token over the same directory; 1.0 means the guard never fired. Line-1 census counts every top-level *.jsonl once, keyed on presence of a top-level cwd field in the first physical line.
checks.note: The claim's statement about Claude Code holds - the map is many-to-one and the harness does not disambiguate below the cap. The csift half has drifted out from under it, and this is the most actionable finding in the area. The stated reason for reading only line 1 is a performance one - 'the cwd field sits in the first record's first ~200 bytes' - and that premise is now false for 100% of the corpus. A fix should scan the first few lines, or the first line carrying a message field, rather than exactly one; the bounded 64 KiB head read already covers the extra lines. Note also that the ledger's own instrument for this claim is unsound as written: distinct cwd values inside one directory prove nothing about collisions, because the deep-cd case in PATH-009 produces them too - the encodings must be compared, not the cwd strings.

claims.behavior: The transcript writer and the project-directory encoder handle astral-plane characters by OPPOSITE conventions: the writer emits them verbatim as 4-byte UTF-8 and never as an escaped surrogate pair (over the whole live corpus - 66 top-level transcripts, 803,946 lines - 8,633 lines, 1.074%, carry a 4-byte UTF-8 lead byte in 0xF0-0xF4, and 0 lines carry a real `\udXXX` surrogate escape; exactly 1 line matches a naive surrogate regex, but its backslash run is EVEN, so those six characters are literal text quoted inside a tool result rather than an escape the writer produced), while the cwd encoder counts the same character as TWO UTF-16 code units and emits TWO dashes into the directory name.
claims.depends: csift must not carry either rule across: the verbatim-UTF-8 transcript convention is what keeps a non-ASCII (emoji, CJK) needle prefilter-eligible against raw line bytes - the needle-safety predicate escapes only `"`, C0 controls and DEL - while the same emoji sitting in a cwd must be re-encoded unit-wise by `path::encode_cwd` to two dashes or the project directory is not found. Applying the encoder's UTF-16 view to search needles, or the writer's codepoint view to the encoder, breaks one surface silently in each direction.
claims.instrument: Writer side: python over every `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` - count a line if any of its raw bytes is in 0xF0..=0xF4, and separately if a match of `\\u[dD][89abAB][0-9a-fA-F]{2}` is preceded by an ODD run of consecutive backslash bytes (the parity guard is required: without it the corpus returns 1 false positive, a doubled backslash in quoted content). Counting rule: one observation per whole line, not prefix-bounded. Whole-corpus rather than a random sample, so a stranger reruns the identical number. Measured 2026-09-02 at CC 2.1.258: 803,946 lines, 8,633 four-byte-lead lines, 0 real surrogate escapes. Encoder side: `strings -n 6 <cc-binary> | rg -o 'function k\(e\)\{return e\.replace\(/\[\^a-zA-Z0-9\]/g,"-"\)\}.{0,300}'` recovers the sanitizer and its >200-cap wrapper, the `"projects"` path builder shows that wrapper is what names the project directory, a search for a unicode-flag variant (`/gu`, `/ug`, `/gv`) returns zero matches, and evaluating the extracted regex in a JS engine yields two dashes for one astral character against one dash for one BMP character. The csift unit test `encode_matches_cc_exactly_on_non_ascii_and_windows_paths` (src/path/tests/encode.rs) then pins the same law crate-side, but it is a regression guard on csift, not an instrument on Claude Code.

claims.behavior: Entering Plan Mode makes Claude Code write a type:"attachment" record whose attachment payload is minted by ONE literal (165739354): {type:"plan_mode", reminderType:"full"|"sparse", isSubAgent:<bool>, planFilePath:"<absolute path>", planExists:<bool>} plus up to FIVE optional keys - customInstructions and workshopDocPath (present only when their sources are defined) and the three conditional spreads workshopOfferDocPath, workshopActiveDocPath and prototypeOffer:true. The collector runs once per submitted prompt inside the prompt-submit attachment phase (169789218) and is registered as one labelled collector in the attachment aggregator (165731479); it returns nothing unless the permission mode is plan, and returns nothing again while a plan_mode attachment was already emitted fewer than TURNS_BETWEEN_ATTACHMENTS turns ago (165738400), which is why a long plan session carries only a handful of these records rather than one per turn. reminderType is computed from the count of plan_mode attachments since the last exit and a workshop-doc change (165738817). The session plan slug is minted or read immediately BEFORE the payload is built (165738620) and the record envelope stamps it, so the record carries a top-level slug and planFilePath is always "<slug>.md". The payload is wrapped into the transcript record by the attachment wrapper {attachment, type:"attachment", uuid, timestamp} (165765262). This attachment is the AUTHORITATIVE binding and takes precedence, but it is not the ONLY binding: when no plan_mode attachment exists Claude Code falls back to the first-valid-slug law (PLAN-006). Measured over the whole projects root on 2026-09-04 (one parse pass over every non-journal *.jsonl, one row per attachment record keyed on the PARSED attachment.type): 21 plan_mode records, 23 plan_mode_exit, 2 plan_mode_reentry; all 21 plan_mode payloads share ONE key set - isSubAgent, planExists, planFilePath, reminderType, type - so none of the five optional keys has a specimen in this corpus; 21/21 carry a top-level slug and 21/21 have basename(planFilePath) == "<slug>.md".
claims.depends: csift binds a session's plan to the planFilePath of the latest plan_mode attachment rather than guessing a path from the slug, so a path-shaped guess can never mis-attribute edits to another session's plan. The byte prefilter token plan_mode also admits the sibling attachment types the same collector emits - plan_mode_reentry (165738742) and plan_mode_exit (165739801) - which likewise carry planFilePath; src/plan.rs then drops them with an exact att.get("type") == Some("plan_mode") check, so the binding stays correct. Measured 2026-09-04: 18 transcripts carry a plan_mode* attachment and 0 of the 18 carry an exit or reentry attachment without a plan_mode one, so the extra prefilter candidates never change an answer. The five optional keys are inert for csift - it reads only planFilePath - but a payload carrying one of them must still parse, which the tolerant attachment model gives free.

claims.behavior: Claude Code folds settings from a fixed FIVE-scope cascade, in order: userSettings, projectSettings, localSettings, flagSettings, policySettings (the source array at 157403765; the selector at 157430948 filters that array and always re-adds the last two, never reordering). The fold runs one accumulator over the scopes in that order with a merge whose customizer returns undefined for a plain scalar (157455238), so a scope read LATER overwrites a scalar such as plansDirectory set earlier - i.e. a --settings flag file and a managed policy file both override user, project and local. Each scope anchors its file differently (157435647): user under the config home, project and policy at the cwd, local at the canonical git root when there is one. The plans-directory resolver (159250888) reads the merged value, joins a relative value to the process's current project cwd through the same getter that stamps every record's top-level cwd (157582764: the async-local cwd, else the project cwd, the original cwd only when that getter throws), refuses a result that escapes that cwd (159251264), and falls back to join(config-home,'plans') (159250345). The resolved directory is memoized on first access, so the binding follows the cwd as it stood early in the session, before any tracked-shell cd moved the per-record value. Specimen (2026-09-03): all 21 plan_mode attachments in the corpus, across 18 transcripts, name the fallback directory; no scope on this host sets plansDirectory, so the configured branch has no on-disk specimen here.
claims.depends: csift's slug-only binding calls plans_dir(root) with root = the transcript's FIRST recorded cwd (src/plan/slug.rs first_cwd, the earliest instant csift can observe), reads user, project and local in that precedence from that root, joins and containment-checks against it, and falls back to <claude-home>/plans. Before v0.10.2 the root was the slug-carrying record's own cwd, which can already have drifted into a subdirectory: the plan file was then joined under the subdirectory and a project-scope plansDirectory was silently dropped. Two known divergences follow from the five-scope cascade: csift reads only the three FILE scopes, so a plansDirectory set in a --settings flag file or in managed policy settings - both of which override all three - is invisible to it; and csift anchors the local scope at the same root it uses for the project scope, whereas the harness anchors local at the canonical git root, so the two disagree when a session's root is not that git root. A session resumed from another directory re-memoizes in the harness, which the first-record instrument cannot see (documented limit).

claims.behavior: csift's `minted_at_compaction` flag means exactly what its code says - the first slug-carrying record is itself a `system`/`compact_boundary` - and it is only ever set on the `slug-only` fallback path. The boundary-first shape has a traced producer: both compaction drivers await the post-compact attachment build gNe (164833974 and 164839486 -> 164850720) BEFORE the boundary record is constructed, and gNe's plan probe p2o (164852199) reaches getPlanFilePath, so a session that has never had a slug gets one MINTED there at its first compaction (the mint itself, and the only place a value enters the map, is at 159247592); the record literal stamps slug:W from the memo of the session id (166105359), which is undefined and therefore omitted before the first mint, so the first carrier is simply the first record written after the first mint. A slug can also be minted during a turn at plan-mode entry (165738400), which is why other transcripts have an attachment, assistant or user record as their first carrier; which mint site ran first for any individual non-boundary-first transcript has not been attributed. Measured 2026-09-02 over the 26 slug-bearing top-level transcripts, the first slug carrier is one of FOUR record types: `assistant` 12, `attachment` 5, `system`/`compact_boundary` 5, `user` 4. Exactly 8 transcripts carry no `plan_mode` attachment at all and therefore bind `slug-only`; of those, 3 are boundary-first (`minted_at_compaction:true`), 1 is assistant-first and 4 are attachment-first (`minted_at_compaction:false`). Same date, two supporting specimens: a boundary-first slug-only transcript with 2,083 slug-bearing records and one distinct value, and an assistant-first transcript with 69,933 slug-bearing records and one distinct value.
claims.depends: csift sets `minted_at_compaction` when the first slug carrier is a compact boundary. It is a positive signal that a slug arrived at a compaction rather than at Plan-Mode entry, but it is NOT a two-way discriminator for whether Plan Mode ran - `binding_source` is what carries that, and a `slug-only` binding with `minted_at_compaction:false` is the common case (5 of 8 measured on 2026-09-02).
